Industry News: Health Sharing vs. Traditional Health Insurance: Which Is Right for You?

📅 20 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (683 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Wellkeptwallet

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that if your family’s ACA premium has jumped again this year, you’re not imagining it, and you’re not alone in looking at alternatives.
  • A health sharing blueprint (sometimes called a health care sharing ministry, or HCSM) is a nonprofit arrangement where members pay a monthly “contribution” that goes toward other members’ eligible medical bills, instead of a premium that goes to an insurance tech giant.
  • Recent findings suggest that tennessee’s Department of Commerce and Insurance is blunt: health care sharing ministries facilitate the sharing of medical expenses and are not insurance companies, and whether anyone helps with your bills is entirely voluntary rather than legally guaranteed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that if your family’s ACA premium has jumped again this year, you’re not imagining it, and you’re not alone in looking at alternatives. Health sharing plans have moved from a faith-based niche into a mainstream budgeting conversation. But before you switch, it’s worth understanding exactly what you’re trading away, not just what you’re saving.

A health sharing blueprint (sometimes called a health care sharing ministry, or HCSM) is a nonprofit arrangement where members pay a monthly “contribution” that goes toward other members’ eligible medical bills, instead of a premium that goes to an insurance tech giant. There’s no insurance contract, and no company is legally on the hook to pay your claims.

Recent findings suggest that tennessee’s Department of Commerce and Insurance is blunt: health care sharing ministries facilitate the sharing of medical expenses and are not insurance companies, and whether anyone helps with your bills is entirely voluntary rather than legally guaranteed. Michigan’s insurance regulator adds that HCSMs aren’t classified as insurance because they don’t assume risk and have no legal obligation to pay members’ costs.

Example: Zion HealthShare is a modern health sharing community that markets itself as a lower-cost alternative to ACA aims, with no provider networks and members paying an “Initial Unshareable Amount” (their version of a deductible) before larger bills become eligible for sharing.

Read our review of Zion HealthShare.

Sources indicate that traditional health insurance is a regulated contract, an ACA marketplace proposal, an employer plan, or a private major-medical policy. The insurer must pay covered claims, cover pre-existing conditions from day one, and include the ACA’s essential health benefits (preventive care, maternity, mental health, and more), a distinction healthinsurance.org explains in detail when comparing HCSMs with ACA-compliant coverage.

In a recent development, solo Health is another option built for self-employed people. It’s a self-funded major medical health strategy with a nationwide PPO network, and it works differently from both health sharing and ACA Marketplace coverage. Eligibility is based on a short health questionnaire. Read our full Solo Health review.

Employer-sponsored family premiums averaged $26,993 in 2025, and many 2026 ACA marketplace aims are seeing median premium hikes of 18–20% as subsidies shrink and medical costs climb. By comparison, health sharing contributions often run $150–$400 per person per month, roughly 30–50% less.

But that gap exists because health sharing plans aren’t required to guarantee anything. Traditional insurers already deny 19–20% of claims on average (some carriers reportedly higher), so even “real” insurance isn’t friction-free, but at least it comes with legal appeal rights and state oversight. A health share’s review process is informal and ministry-specific, with no equivalent legal backstop if a bill gets rejected.

Recent findings suggest that it works best for generally healthy families who don’t qualify for meaningful ACA subsidies, are comfortable handling more paperwork and negotiating bills themselves, and want lower fixed monthly costs in exchange for taking on more risk. It’s a weaker fit for anyone managing a chronic condition, planning a pregnancy, or who needs the legal certainty of a regulated contract.

According to recent reports, health sharing can meaningfully lower your monthly healthcare costs, but the trade-off is real: you’re giving up the legal guarantee, essential-benefit mandates, and regulatory protection that come with traditional insurance. For a healthy family stretched thin by rising ACA premiums, it can be a reasonable bridge option. For anyone with ongoing medical needs, the savings usually aren’t worth the uncertainty.

Is a health sharing initiative the same as a health insurance policy?No. It’s a voluntary cost-sharing arrangement, not a legally binding insurance contract.

Can I use a health sharing proposal and still contribute to an HSA?Not based on the health share alone; you also need to be enrolled in a genuine HDHP to be HSA-eligible.

Will a health sharing blueprint cover a pre-existing condition?Usually only after a waiting period, which varies by organization, often 12 to 36 months.

Does the ACA’s individual mandate penalty apply if I only have a health share?No, the federal individual mandate penalty was eliminated starting in 2019, so this isn’t a factor either way.

“Until he got all rich and fancy so that he no longer understands the common person’s plight.

Stash probably doesn’t even practice any of these money-saving things he preaches any more!”.

When I read things like this, I can’t help but laugh. Because on the one hand, when you put a bunch of personal life details online like this, being misunderstood is just part of the package. But on the other hand, if the critics could peek in and see our real lives – not just mine but those of all the Mustachians – they would have to give up their conspiracy theories and accept the fact that this stuff just works.

Because really, not much has changed when it comes to the basics. Like many MMM readers over the past twelve years, my total wealth level has increased pretty regularly. But also like many of us, I haven’t felt the need to change very much about my spending because I was doing my best to live an enjoyable life in the first place.

It has been revealed that how have so many people found such great success? I think we Mustachians have something that’s a bit more rare and special than standard financial advice, which is what makes it work so well:.

Sources indicate that standard Advice: Slash your spending and make sacrifices until you reach a certain savings percentage, and beyond that it doesn’t matter, it’s all personal choice. More income? Great, that means you don’t have to sacrifice as much! FatFIRE for everyone!

Mustachianism: Cultivate a love of efficiency, creativity, self awareness, and self improvement. Use this knowledge to improve your life in all ways, including those which help you live better even as your monthly expense rate drops over time.

So what does this mean in practice?

According to recent reports, well, I’ll give you some examples from my own present-day life. Things I do because I happen to enjoy them, which also happen to save a lot of money. Some of these are normal, some are silly and may end up in some future gossip magazine hit piece, but all of them happen to work for me, so the critics can be damned.

Sources indicate that as I list each item, I’ll include an estimate of how much the activity saves me per decade, because you should always think at least in terms of decades. To make that calculation yourself, just use the “rule of 172” – take a monthly expense and multiply it by 172 to estimate how much it would compound into over ten years, if invested.

1) Fixing my own House (and everybody else’s too).

According to recent reports, I’m a big believer in self-sufficiency, and working to build up the skills to manage the most notable parts of your own life without depending on too many things (or people) that are outside of your control. In other words, one giant recipe for a happy life is simply to Become a Producer of the Things You Most Enjoy Consuming.

Industry observers note that and in my case, I happen to love houses. I like living in beautiful, functional spaces and sharing them with friends. But most houses are ugly and poorly designed when you buy them, so I realized that I also love solving problems and redesigning old buildings to become upcoming again. I enjoy this process so much that I spend most of my free time doing it – on both my own properties and the homes of friends.

And I love teaching other people to gain power over their own houses too. It’s amazing how great people feel as they lose their fear and dependence on outside contractors, and gain the ability to fix and maintain things with their own two hands.

Savings: An average of $20,000 per year = $287,000 per decade.

You know what’s great? Having so much money that you can buy whatever you want – high quality things which get delivered to your front door the very next day.

According to recent reports, you know what’s even better? Not buying some of those new things, and instead finding ways to share, repurpose and buy equally high quality items from other people who don’t need them any more. All while building up your own community and creating new friendships in the process.

Craigslist, Facebook Marketplace, and even NextDoor all have Buy Nothing groups for most areas. In the MMM-HQ community, we run a Discord server with about 200 local people, who chat around the clock on a wide range of subjects. They help each other with major projects in one channel called #diyhowto, and give away and sell things on #forsale and #buynothing.

Although our private Discord group is my favorite, I also use Craigslist regularly, and probably save (and earn) a few thousand every year thanks to the habit:.

Savings: About $42,000 per decade.

Industry observers note that we all know that Mr. Money Mustache’s biggest contribution to personal finance is to insist that bike transportation is the best way to get around. And I still feel this way. As we learned in The True Cost of Commuting, cars cost at least 50 cents per mile to operate, while bikes are much cheaper, mainly due to reduced depreciation and maintenance costs (which are even bigger than the gas savings).

Industry observers note that I do still use bikes (or walking) for at least 95% of my local trips these days, but because I live in the center of a small city, my life is pretty local. So this still only adds up to about 2000 miles per year, a savings of “only” $14,000 per decade.

But when you choose active transportation, there’s much more to the picture than just cutting your car expenses. You’re changing everything about your physical and mental health picture for the better, which brings us to the next point of….

Industry observers note that although I’m no competitive athlete, whenever I see an option to make my body work a bit harder, I usually take it. Stairs instead of elevators, running the golf course instead of using a golf cart, moving my own furniture and appliances instead of calling a mover, shoveling snow and raking leaves instead of using a machine.

It has been revealed that when I face a decision like this, I simply ask myself the question: “Well, Mustache. Do you want MORE health and fitness, or LESS?” Putting it in that context makes the answer obvious. Every bit helps, because when it comes to your body, the rule is pretty much use it or lose it.

But how much money does this save? There’s no real way to calculate it exactly, but I like to think of it this way: The US average health care spending is about $13,000 per person per year. My lifetime costs due to illness or medication so far have been just about zero, plus I know I’ve had more energy and greater productivity due to being healthy. Let’s just put it very conservatively and set the estimated savings and benefits at $10k per year which means.

Estimated Savings:  $140,000 per decade.

5) Saving Energy by Running my home like a Glamping Retreat.

Here’s where things get a bit silly, but my level of joy is actually at its greatest.

My personality type is probably a weird combination of an engineer, a carpenter, an artsy hippie, and a mad scientist. Oh, and a devoted homebody too. Because of this, my favorite activity most days is to just run around my house taking care of things and trying new little experiments and improvements.

Sometimes I’ll cut a few substantial holes on on the South side of the house and install sliding doors and big windows to allow nice sunbeams and passive solar energy to get into my house and give me free heat in the winters. Other times it’s just smaller things to save energy and live more at at one with the seasons of my area:.

It has been revealed that even taken all together, these things are pretty small – the average combined gas and electric bill for my area is about $250 per month, while my usage adds up to about $75. So while we’re only saving about $30,000 per decade for what sounds like a lot of work to most people, I consider this to be the biggest win because I enjoy living in “MMM’s Energy Efficiency Playground” so much.

6) Local Living over Constant Travel.

“Hey, we’re having a major back yard pool party next weekend to celebrate Amy’s graduation from kindergarten, can you make it?”.

Recent findings suggest that “OH NOOOO!!! We will be off in at Disneyland that whole week! We planned the trip months ago, I wish we could make it!

As I type this in the height of the summer season, I really feel this effect at its fullest: almost all of my friends are off on trips, and my guest suite here at home is almost constantly full. People are traveling a lot, and many of them sound like they wish they could spend a few more of their precious summer weeks and weekends at home.

According to recent reports, I’ll let you in on a little secret: you can! The trick is saying, “no thanks” more often to plans that involve you being away, and “yes please” to things that let you stay at home. The benefits are numerous:.

Estimated Savings: Even if you replace just two weeks of travel for a family of four, with equivalent time at home you might save $5,000 per year in direct costs and a further $5,000 per year in incidental benefits like the health and local friendships. This would work out to a shocking $143,000 per decade of wealth increase!

According to recent reports, of course, travel is generally a good thing for broadening the life experience of you and your kids. It’s worth spending on, lavishly at times. But the key is to balance it out and be discerning, keeping the most enriching trips and pruning a few off the bottom of the list. And remembering that home time is valuable and healthy too.

Industry observers note that and Whoa! We’ve already built up a huge list and I feel like I was just getting started.

Taken all together, we’ve already detailed things that compound to $656,000 every decade, which already more than double the median wealth that most American seniors have as they cruise nervously into their retirement years – after over 40 years of work!

In a recent development, and now that I’ve been writing this blog for over ten years myself, I can safely say that over $656,000 of even my most recent worth increases are directly attributable to these simple habits. The same ones many of us have been enjoying and preaching about all along, both before and after our retirement dates.

If money is in genuinely short supply, you could go a lot further than the examples in this article. And indeed, there’s a lot more laid out in this blog or the MMM Boot Camp email series.

Recent findings suggest that but one of the points of Mustachianism is that you usually don’t have to try all that hard. Just tweaking your lifestyle to be slightly less ridiculous and more efficient than average is usually all it takes.

Recent findings suggest that in the comments: what are your quirks and frugal indulgences? The things you do now to save money, or things you still do even after it’s no longer about the money? I often wonder how widespread this frugality-just-for-fun is. But since we Humans are a naturally curious and problem solving species in our natural state, I suspect there are many more of us out there.

Tech Report: Aeroplan Stopovers — Two Cities for the Price of One

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2865 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Choosefi

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • One of the highest-value redemptions in travel rewards.
  • It has been revealed that picture this: you're settling into a lie-flat business class seat somewhere over the Atlantic, a glass of something cold in hand, knowing that in 48 hours you'll be waking up in Istanbul — and then, a few days later, continuing onward to Bangkok.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

One of the highest-value redemptions in travel rewards.

It has been revealed that picture this: you're settling into a lie-flat business class seat somewhere over the Atlantic, a glass of something cold in hand, knowing that in 48 hours you'll be waking up in Istanbul — and then, a few days later, continuing onward to Bangkok. Two bucket-list cities. One award booking. One points balance. This is what the Aeroplan stopover sweet spot feels like in practice. It's not a trick or a loophole — it's a deliberately designed feature of Air Canada's Aeroplan program that the vast majority of travelers simply don't know exists. And that gap between awareness and reality is exactly where the ChooseFI community finds its edge. Here's the math that should make your jaw drop. A business class itinerary from North America to Istanbul with a continuing flight onward to Bangkok — two long-haul segments, lie-flat seats, Star Alliance lounges at every connection — would cost somewhere between **$6,000 and $15,000 in cash**. That's a realistic retail range depending on season and how far out you book. Most people never consider it a possibility for a family vacation or a milestone trip because the sticker price puts it in a different universe. With Aeroplan, you're booking that same itinerary — the same seats, the same lounges, the same Turkish Airlines or Thai Airways product — for **75,000 Aeroplan points**. At the low end of the cash price range, that's already **8 cents per point**. At the high end, you're extracting **20 cents per point** from a currency that most people earned by putting groceries on a credit card. The pricing inefficiency here is structural. Aeroplan's partner award chart prices long-haul business class at a fixed rate regardless of cash fare fluctuations. When business class prices spike — around holidays, during peak travel seasons, during major events — your points cost stays exactly the same. You're insulated from the market. That's the FI mindset applied to travel: you've already paid for the trip in points, slowly accumulated through everyday spending, and now you're simply redeeming the stored value. The stopover itself is nearly free. Aeroplan charges just 5,000 extra miles to add a stopover city to a one-way award. That means your Istanbul layover becomes a multi-day stay — at zero additional points cost beyond that small add-on — and you haven't booked a second award at all. One booking. Two destinations. That's the entire premise, and once you see it, you can't unsee it.

The mechanism behind this sweet spot is elegantly simple once you understand it, but it requires knowing three things that most travelers don't: how Aeroplan's routing rules work, what a stopover actually is in the context of an award ticket, and why Star Alliance's global network makes this scalable to almost any destination pair you can imagine.

It has been revealed that when Aeroplan relaunched its loyalty program in 2020, it did something remarkable: it eliminated fuel surcharges entirely and published a partner award chart with fixed pricing for flights on Star Alliance carriers. This is critical. When you book Turkish Airlines business class through Aeroplan, you pay the Aeroplan fixed chart rate — not what Turkish Airlines would charge in its own currency or miles program, and not the inflated cash price. That fixed chart is the engine of this redemption.

For long-haul international business class, Aeroplan's chart prices routing through multiple regions based on your origin and destination — not every intermediate stop. This is the aha moment. Aeroplan determines your award price based on where your journey starts and where it ends, and then allows you to add a stopover in between for just 5,000 additional miles. The stopover city is priced as a pass-through for the purpose of calculating your award zone, not as a second trip.

According to recent reports, on a one-way Aeroplan award, you're permitted to add a free stopover — meaning you can stay in an intermediate city for any length of time before continuing to your final destination. That 5,000-mile add-on is essentially the cost of a full additional destination. Compare that to booking a second one-way award from Istanbul to Bangkok, which would cost you another 40,000–55,000 Aeroplan points in business class. The math is decisive.

Industry observers note that the routing must be geographically sensible — you can't fly backwards across the globe — but Aeroplan's allowance for multi-segment itineraries through Star Alliance hubs gives you enormous flexibility. Istanbul (IST) is a Turkish Airlines hub. Bangkok (BKK) is served by Thai Airways and several Star Alliance carriers. Both are Star Alliance partners. Both are bookable through Aeroplan at fixed chart rates with no fuel surcharges.

Sources indicate that the best part for the ChooseFI community is how accessible the underlying points are. Aeroplan accepts transfers from four major programs:.

Chase's instant transfer speed is particularly valuable here. When you find business class availability — which can disappear swiftly — you want to move points immediately. Having Chase Ultimate Rewards as your primary earning currency means you can search, find space, and transfer points before the availability window closes. The 1:1 ratio across all four programs means no conversion math — every point you earn translates directly to one Aeroplan mile.

According to recent reports, booking an Aeroplan stopover award in business class is genuinely one of the more complex redemptions in the travel rewards world, but it becomes manageable when you break it into distinct phases. Here's exactly how to do it.

Start by deciding on your two destinations. Aeroplan stopovers work best when your intermediate city is a major Star Alliance hub that lies geographically between your origin and final destination. Classic combinations include North America to Istanbul (Turkish Airlines hub) continuing to Southeast Asia, or North America to a European hub continuing to the Middle East or East Africa. Your stopover city should be somewhere you genuinely want to spend 2–5 days — this is a real trip, not just a layover.

Sources indicate that this is the most crucial and most time-consuming step. You need to find saver-level business class availability on both segments independently before you book.

Once you've confirmed availability on both segments, go to aeroplan.com and use the multi-city search function. Enter your full itinerary — origin, stopover city with your intended layover dates, and final destination.

Once you've confirmed the award is bookable and are ready to complete the reservation:.

Sources indicate that complete your booking on aeroplan.com or with a phone agent, confirm the stopover is properly reflected in your itinerary, and save every confirmation email. Verify your seats on each carrier's website immediately after booking.

A stopover is an intentional break in your journey lasting more than 24 hours at a connecting city. Most airlines treat stopovers as separate tickets, charging full price for each segment. Aeroplan is one of the few programs that allows a free stopover on round-trip awards, letting you explore a connecting city for days before continuing to your final destination. This is fundamentally different from a layover, which is a brief connection of a few hours at an airport. The stopover must be in a city served by a Star Alliance carrier on your routing, and the key is that Aeroplan prices the entire itinerary as one award, not two.

Card links may earn ChooseFI a commission. See our advertiser disclosure.

Let's build a real example so you can see exactly what this looks like on paper — and in the air.

The Route: Toronto (YYZ) → Istanbul (IST, 4-day stopover) → Bangkok (BKK) The Carrier: Turkish Airlines business class on both segments The Points Cost: 75,000 Aeroplan miles for the two segments + 5,000 miles for the stopover = 80,000 Aeroplan miles total Cash Equivalent: A comparable business class itinerary on this routing typically retails for $9,000–$12,000 in 2026, depending on when you search and how far in advance you book.

The CPP Calculation: At the midpoint cash value of $10,500 against 80,000 points, you're extracting 13.1 cents per Aeroplan mile — well inside the 8–20 cent range this sweet spot delivers, and roughly 10–13 times the value of redeeming Aeroplan miles for cash back.

Recent findings suggest that the Turkish Airlines business class product on long-haul routes is consistently rated among the top business class experiences in the Star Alliance network. On the YYZ–IST segment — operated on a 787 or A330 — you'll have access to a lie-flat seat with direct aisle access, the Turkish Airlines Lounge in Istanbul (widely considered one of the best airport lounges in the world, full stop), and a meal service that reflects the airline's culinary reputation. The IST lounge alone — with its restaurant, spa, golf simulator, and sleeping areas — is worth lingering in even before your onward connection.

Industry observers note that in Istanbul, your four days might include the Hagia Sophia at sunrise, a Bosphorus dinner cruise, and the Grand Bazaar before you head to the airport to continue your journey. You've paid nothing additional for this stay beyond the 5,000-mile stopover fee.

The IST–BKK segment puts you into Bangkok in the evening, ready for Thailand's extraordinary food, culture, and cost of living — which, for the FI-minded traveler, means your lodging and meals on the ground are remarkably affordable, stretching the value of your trip even further.

Sources indicate that total points cost for two lie-flat business class segments and a full European city stay: 80,000 miles, earned on everyday credit card spending. That's the entire proposition, and those numbers are real.

Industry observers note that book at exactly 355 days out. Aeroplan opens its booking window at 355 days before departure. The best business class availability on popular routes — especially Turkish Airlines long-haul — appears at this window and gets claimed promptly. Set a calendar reminder and be ready to search at the 355-day mark for your target travel dates.

Use Chase Ultimate Rewards as your primary earning currency for this redemption. The instant transfer speed to Aeroplan is genuinely differentiating. When you find award space and need to move quickly, Chase lets you transfer and book in the same session. Amex, Capital One, and Bilt all require 1–2 days, during which your availability can evaporate.

Sources indicate that search availability before you transfer points. Confirm space exists on every segment before a single point moves. There's no undo button on a transfer, and Aeroplan points sitting idle in your account are fine — points transferred to an account where you can't find availability are a headache.

Call Aeroplan for complex routings. The online multi-city tool is functional but can struggle with nuanced stopover configurations. Phone agents are experienced with these bookings and have the same access to inventory. The call is worth it for an $80,000-point booking.

Recent findings suggest that leverage the open-jaw rule too. Aeroplan also allows open-jaw routing — fly into one city, depart from another. Combined with the stopover, you can design a route that visits three geographic points on a single award: fly into Istanbul, take trains or ferries to Athens, and fly home from Athens. The award prices the same way.

Don't assume partner availability matches Aeroplan's search. Turkish Airlines and other Star Alliance partners don't always make every seat available through Aeroplan's online portal. If you see space on the carrier's own site but not on aeroplan.com, call — agents can often access inventory the website misses.

Don't book inflexible connecting flights. Long-haul itineraries with tight connections are a risk. Build in at least a 3-hour connection at hub airports to protect against irregular operations that could affect your award segments.

Don't earn Marriott Bonvoy points with this redemption in mind. The 3:1 transfer ratio to Aeroplan makes Marriott a poor choice for funding this specific award. Stick to Amex, Chase, Capital One, or Bilt at 1:1.

Industry observers note that don't book this for a time-sensitive trip. Award availability, transfer timelines, and multi-carrier coordination mean this requires planning runway. Build in at least 3–4 weeks of lead time beyond the actual booking date.

This redemption is purpose-built for the advanced travel rewards enthusiast in the ChooseFI community — someone who has already mastered the basics (earning transferable points, understanding award charts, booking straightforward partner awards) and is ready to unlock the next level of value.

Recent findings suggest that the ideal profile: A couple or solo traveler planning a milestone trip — a significant anniversary, a sabbatical, a once-in-a-decade adventure — who wants to experience two destinations in business class without paying business class prices for either one. You're flexible on travel dates, comfortable spending time on the phone with an airline agent, and genuinely excited about the trip-planning process as part of the experience.

In a recent development, minimum points balance: You'll need approximately 80,000 Aeroplan miles to complete this booking (75,000 for the award plus 5,000 for the stopover). That's achievable from a single premium credit card welcome bonus, a combination of two or three mid-tier welcome bonuses, or 12–18 months of everyday spending on a 2x transferable points card.

This is NOT the right redemption for:.

For the ChooseFI traveler who's been building transferable points for a year or two and wants to see what this system is truly capable of, this redemption is the answer.

In a recent development, pick a final destination and a stopover city on the same Star Alliance routing. Classic combos: Istanbul + Bangkok, Zurich + Tokyo, Vienna + Singapore. The stopover city must be a natural connection point on a Star Alliance route between your origin and destination.

It has been revealed that set a calendar alert for 355 days before your departure date. Search for business class availability on each segment separately using United.com or Aeroplan.com. Both legs need saver-level award space on the same booking.

Before transferring any points, verify that saver award space exists on both the outbound leg (origin to stopover city) and the continuation (stopover city to final destination). If either segment is unavailable, the booking will not work.

Sources indicate that transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards (instant) or Amex Membership Rewards (1-2 days) to your Aeroplan account at a 1:1 ratio. Only transfer once you have confirmed availability on both segments.

Call Aeroplan or use the multi-city search tool online. Specify your stopover city and duration (up to the maximum allowed). The system prices it as one round-trip award. Confirm total points match expectations before completing the booking.

Aeroplan allows stopovers of up to 45 days on round-trip awards. You can stay in your stopover city for a few days or several weeks, giving you genuine time to explore rather than just passing through.

It has been revealed that no, stopovers are only available on round-trip awards through Aeroplan. One-way bookings do not qualify for the free stopover benefit. This is one reason round-trip awards can offer better value than two one-ways.

Aeroplan has improved its online multi-city search tool, and some stopover itineraries can now be booked online. However, complex routings may still require a phone call. When calling, clearly state you want a round-trip award with a stopover and specify your stopover city and dates.

The best stopover cities are Star Alliance hub cities with strong business class availability: Istanbul (Turkish Airlines hub), Zurich (SWISS hub), Vienna (Austrian hub), Singapore (Singapore Airlines hub), and Tokyo (ANA hub). These hubs offer the most consistent saver-level award space.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

According to recent reports, the Aeroplan stopover is one of the most powerful tools in the travel rewards playbook. By adding a free stopover to a round-trip business class award, you can explore two world-class cities for the points cost of visiting one. It requires planning, patience at the 355-day booking window, and comfort with Star Alliance routing rules, but the payoff is extraordinary: 10-15 cents per point in value on experiences that would cost thousands in cash. For the FI community member who has mastered basic award bookings and is ready to level up, this is the redemption that changes how you think about travel.

Six Dumb Misconceptions About The Economy (that the Politicians Want You To Believe)

📅 13 Oct 2024 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2011 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Well, it looks like we’re here in another US election year already.
  • As Advanced Mustachians, we already know that the ongoing battle of Harris vs.
  • But out of all the things the politicians like to bicker about, there’s one area where MMM does need to set the record straight, and that area is of course money.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Well, it looks like we’re here in another US election year already.

As Advanced Mustachians, we already know that the ongoing battle of Harris vs. Trump should not be consuming much of our time. Sure, we do our research and cast our votes but after that we move right on to focus on other things within our own circle of control.

But out of all the things the politicians like to bicker about, there’s one area where MMM does need to set the record straight, and that area is of course money. Your money, the economy in general, and the overall wealth of the nation.

Politicians are already not known for being the sharpest tools in the shed when it comes to technical stuff like science, technology, or economics. But this year the discourse has become particularly dumb, as our candidates try to manipulate undecided voters in swing states with ideas that are based on irrational emotions rather than sound economic sense.

For one particularly funny example, you may have noticed that the competing party (Trump in this case) is attacking the incumbents (Biden/Harris) over the “bad economy.” When in fact the US economy is stronger than it has ever been, with the lowest unemployment we’ve ever seen as well.

It’s hard to imagine a better situation than we have right now, and in fact the recent bout of higher inflation is a sign that things have been going too well, and we needed to step on the brakes with the help of higher interest rates.

It has been revealed that but somehow the people still seem to believe that we have a “bad” economy. Take a look at this Gallup poll showing that while most people (85%) are doing really well right now, they assume that it’s just their own good fortune – only 17% believe the economy is doing well.

This is mathematically impossible, because if most people are doing well, that’s the definition of a good economy! And suspiciously enough, this widespread wrongness correlates quite nicely with the rise of social media misinformation.

So the politicians and the news have been doing the opposite of what they should be doing in an ideal situation (sharing accurate information). And sure, we can always just ignore their speeches and go on with our lives. But when it comes to economics, knowledge is power (and money). The more accurately we understand how things really work, the wealthier we will all become.

So with all that in mind, I hereby present you with my list of the….

Top Dumb Things Politicians Want You To Believe About The Economy.

1: The President Controls the Economy.

Recent findings suggest that if there’s a recession, the opposition party likes to blame it on the current president. If the economy is booming, the current president likes to give himself (or possibly soon herself) credit for all of that success. But really, the US economy is way too substantial – and thankfully way too free – for the president to control or really even influence all that strongly.

In reality, our economy is a gigantic machine which converts labor and materials into things like iPhones, hospitals and pumpkin pies. And although we’re the biggest economy at 26% of the planet, we are still heavily influenced by that much bigger 74% of economic activity that the other 7.6 billion people on Earth are busy producing everywhere else.

When we have our inevitable little boom and bust cycles, they are mostly caused by the normal cycle of irrational exuberance (and greed) like the 2007 housing boom, followed by brief periods of extreme fear and pessimism like the 2008-2012 financial and housing crash.

According to recent reports, the government does play a role too, by setting tax rates and other rules. But the effects of these policies are usually so delayed and unpredictable, that you can’t draw a straight line between today’s president and today’s economy. In other words, the government does its best to adjust the rudder on our giant ship, but in the short term our economy lurches around on the waves and storms of the ocean.

2: The President Controls Interest Rates.

According to recent reports, this one is especially funny to me, as our candidates feign sympathy for the hard life of middle class Americans, who now face higher borrowing costs on their credit cards and car loans and mortgages. They claim they will fight to bring the interest rates down. Trump even goes as far as bullying our Federal Reserve board members (who can only do their jobs if we allow them to function as independent experts) and suggesting that he would take over the whole department, if elected.

The real story is that while monetary policy would be a terrible tool to leave in the hands of a sitting president (see Argentina), it does function as an excellent set of gas and brake pedals for the economy if used properly. When things slow down and unemployment gets too high, a cut to the interest rates will produce a boost in everything from new jobs to stock prices. But if things get too hot, you get rapid inflation which can mess up the system.

3: Inflation has Made Life Harder for Americans (and the President Can Magically Reverse it).

Sources indicate that this line of reasoning is even dumber than the last one. For a couple of years after the Covid era, we had rapid inflation. It was caused by a rare combination of a goods shortage caused by things like factory closures and remote work, plentiful demand from government stimulus spending and low interest rates. These factors have since ironed themselves out, and inflation is back down to an ultra-low 2.4%.

Industry observers note that but most significantly, wages have still risen faster than inflation so we are all better off than before! Since 2019, overall prices are up 19% and our wages are up 21%. So even after all that inflation, we are still doing just fine. But the candidates are still bickering over inflation as if it’s an actual problem, and even worse promising to “bring prices back down”. And they’ve managed to convince the electorate that “higher wages and prices” is the same thing as “a bad economy”. Which is just plain wrong.

Bonus dumbness: politicians also occasionally blame “greedy corporations” for increasing prices to hoard profits. While price increases are totally acceptable in a market system (as a business owner you are free to set prices wherever you like), in reality it doesn’t usually happen because our markets are too competitive. For example, a recent deep analysis from NPR showed that no, grocery stores haven’t made any windfall profit at all off of this recent bout of Covid-fueled inflation.

4: The President Controls Housing Prices.

It has been revealed that one important thing that has changed over the past ten years is that US house prices and rents have both risen much faster than general inflation and even wages. On the positive side, interest rates have also risen which tends to make houses feel more expensive and is supposed to help bring house prices down. But it hasn’t happened yet which means we have the double whammy of higher prices and higher interest costs for mortgage borrowers.

The dumb part is that our candidates are proposing things that would make the problem even worse, like subsidies for first-time homebuyers or schemes to reduce the interest rates. When really the solution is to increase the supply of housing, which I personally think will happen if we stop putting up roadblocks for homebuilders (myself included) to build housing.

Things like faster and cheaper permits, less onerous and expensive building codes, eliminating suburban-style zoning and setback and car parking rules, and changing laws so that NIMBYs no longer get any say over what other people do with their own land could all help reduce the cost of building a house by about 50%, quickly and permanently.

5: The President Controls Gas Prices, and They Are At the moment “High” and We Want Them Lower.

Sources indicate that ahh, gasoline! The most ridiculous of things to worry about and the fuel for many of MMM’s rants since 2011.

First of all, on an inflation-adjusted basis, gasoline is still about the same price as it was in 1950: in the $3-4 range per gallon, in today’s dollars.

Recent findings suggest that secondly, it is so cheap that even with our huge inefficient American vehicles, the average household is still only spending 2.5% of their disposable income on the stuff! (The funny part is that they spend many times more on the rest of the car ownership experience while thinking gas is the part that is expensive).

Recent findings suggest that third, gasoline has been obsolete for almost a decade now. You can get a used electric car for less than the price of a comparable used gas car, or if you’re a fancypants money waster like me, fresh EVs are also cheaper than their gas counterparts. You get a faster, nicer car that almost never needs maintenance OR gasoline, and save money.

So why are we even still talking about this antique fuel of a previous era? Why aren’t the candidates also arguing over the price of Kodak film or typewriters or fax machines?

6: The Economy is Something We Should Even Worry About.

In a recent development, the funniest part about all this economic talk is that we’re focusing on the wrong thing. While hard work and business and advancing the frontiers of human knowledge are all fun things, the reality is that we passed the point of having “Enough” decades ago. When the American middle class complains about how hard we have it these days, it’s like a bunch of overfed people at a buffet wishing they could just have one more flavor of donuts stacked onto the table.

Recent findings suggest that yes, we have income and wealth inequality so that the rich tend to get richer more promptly. And yes, we should keep that in check with a somewhat progressive tax system because a more equal society tends to be a more peaceful and happy one.

Industry observers note that but have you noticed that as the rich people get richer, they don’t get any happier? It’s because after you pass the point of “Enough”, adding more money doesn’t really help much.

In a recent development, and “Enough” is much more defined by your mindset (and your collection of life skills) than your paycheck. So if the politicians really cared about improving our happiness and wellbeing, they’d be preaching the Principles of Mustachianism rather than pandering to the specific requests of coal miners or billionaires.

Sources indicate that but alas, winning an election is a very different thing than proposing stuff that is actually best for the country. And for that reason, we cast our votes for the best party and then tune back out until the next election.

In the Comments: Has the election season been getting you down, pumping you up, or just giving you a thorough dose of “Meh”?

It has been revealed that while researching economic stats for this article, I came across a quirky but informative series of videos called USA Facts by none other than former Microsoft CEO Steve Ballmer. It seems that he had the same frustration as me: Americans are fighting over a bunch of opinions and misinformation without even bothering to look up the actual facts. So he made a well-produced series of videos that just share the facts without the baggage of political hype on top of them. I wish our politicians could do the same thing!

It has been revealed that from its humble beginnings in 2008 to today, Bitcoin’s history has been relatively short but very eventful. The original protocol for this popular digital currency was created in 2008 by Satoshi Nakamoto, believed to be a pseudonym for an unknown developer or group of developers.

Nakamoto launched the Bitcoin network just a year later and began mining the currency— an estimated 1 million bitcoins were mined in the early years.

The creator(s) of this first-of-its-kind asset developed the cryptocurrency in response to the Great Recession of 2007-2009, spurred by a distrust of the traditional banking system and concerns about its stability.

Given the recent values of Bitcoin, it’s hard to believe the currency first started trading on exchanges in 2010 at under $0.10. Since then, it’s experienced astronomical growth and some pretty wild price swings.

At its most recent high, one bitcoin was worth over $64,000—a far cry from trading for pennies in its earliest days.

Sources indicate that whether you’re thinking of investing in Bitcoin or you’ve held this cryptocurrency for several years, it’s fun to look back at this groundbreaking asset’s history. Read on for insights on Bitcoin milestones, historical returns, and how its returns compare to those of other assets.

Recent findings suggest that since being created, Bitcoin has experienced several milestones. Here’s a look back at some of the most significant moments in the short history of this cryptocurrency:.

Recent findings suggest that while Bitcoin isn’t exempt from the volatility cryptocurrencies often experience, it’s delivered some impressive returns over the years. Here’s a look at Bitcoin’s annual returns from 2010 to 2022:.

And here’s a look at monthly returns, if you feel like getting a deeper dive:.

In a recent development, while Bitcoin has experienced some wild monthly price swings and a couple of years where its value has declined, you can see that its declines have been eclipsed by some incredible gains. Now let’s explore how Bitcoin’s value has changed over 10, 5, 3, and 1 years.

According to recent reports, let’s say you bought one bitcoin on August, 3rd 2013, for $1,106.75, its price at the time. If you held that one bitcoin until August 3rd, 2023, it would’ve been worth $29,310.44, and your total ROI for the 10 years would be 2,546.8%.

We’ll also assume you purchased one Bitcoin for this example. A single bitcoin was valued at $965.31 on August, 3rd, 2018, and its value climbed to $29,310.44 by August 2023. Using our calculation above, your total ROI for those five years would be 294.1%.

A single bitcoin was valued at $11,246.20 in August 2020, and its value climbed to $29,310.44 at the end of 2021. Your total ROI for those three years would be 160.6%.

If you purchased a single bitcoin in August 2022, you would’ve paid around $22,626.83. In one year, that value would’ve increased to $29,310.44. Your total returns for that year would be 29.54%.

Instead of buying one bitcoin, let’s say you decided to invest $1,000 into Bitcoin. Here’s a look at how this $1,000 investment would’ve performed if you bought and held your Bitcoin for 10, 5, 3, and 1 years.

While Bitcoin’s earliest investors would have benefitted the most from buying and holding their Bitcoin, those who’ve invested recently also fared well.

If you’re curious how Bitcoin returns compare to those of other asset classes, here’s how its annual and total returns compare to gold, real estate, and the S&P 500.(Spoiler alert: Bitcoin outperformed all three assets by an enormous margin.).

Industry observers note that if you compare Bitcoin’s returns to gold’s returns, you’ll notice a stark difference. Bitcoin has an average annual return of 1,576% and a total return of 18,912% from 2010 to 2022, while SPDR Gold Shares had an average annual return of just 5.14% and a total return of 61.67% over the same period.

Let’s see if real estate fared any better compared to Bitcoin. The cryptocurrency delivered a whopping 1,576% average annual return and an 18,912% total return from 2010 to 2021, while the Vanguard Real Estate ETF had an average annual return of 13.49% and a total return of 161.91% over the same period.

So, real estate saw slightly higher returns than gold, but it still didn’t come close to Bitcoin’s returns.

The S&P 500 didn’t fare too much better in its head-to-head with Bitcoin. From 2011 to 2023, the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF delivered an average annual return of 15.74% and a total return of 173.14%. While those numbers aren’t too shabby, Bitcoin’s average annual return for the same period was a whopping 819%, and its total return was 9,012%.

With its longevity and astronomically high returns, Bitcoin has been worth the risk for many investors—especially early adopters.

Avianca LifeMiles → Star Alliance Premium Cabin

💡 Key Takeaways
  • One of the cheapest ways to fly Star Alliance business and first class.
  • Picture this: you settle into a Lufthansa Boeing 747-8 business class seat on the upper deck, somewhere over the Atlantic, a glass of Champagne in hand, your fully flat bed already made up behind you.
  • The core insight here is understanding why Avianca LifeMiles prices Star Alliance awards so aggressively — and then understanding how to get points into the program promptly enough to actually use them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the cheapest ways to fly Star Alliance business and first class.

Points for Business/First Class.

Picture this: you settle into a Lufthansa Boeing 747-8 business class seat on the upper deck, somewhere over the Atlantic, a glass of Champagne in hand, your fully flat bed already made up behind you. Latest York to Frankfurt — a route that commands $4,000 to $8,000 in cash for a business class ticket — and you're here for 63,000 Avianca LifeMiles. No fuel surcharges. No carrier-imposed fees eating into your redemption. Just the experience. That's the moment the FI community lives for. Not the luxury itself — though Lufthansa's business class product is genuinely exceptional — but the *math*. The realization that the loyalty system has a pricing gap so wide you could fly a 747 through it. Here's what the numbers actually mean. At the low end, a $4,000 business class ticket redeemed for 63,000 points works out to **6.3 cents per point (CPP)**. At the high end — peak travel season, last-minute pricing, transatlantic demand — that same seat hits $8,000 in cash, which means your LifeMiles are delivering **12.7 cents per point**. For context, most travel rewards experts consider 1–2 CPP a baseline for points value. You're achieving 6 to 12 times that baseline. The reason this feels like a genuine inefficiency rather than just a deal: Avianca LifeMiles prices Star Alliance awards on a **fixed award chart** that doesn't fluctuate with cash fare demand. When airlines raise transatlantic business class fares during summer holidays or major events, your points cost stays exactly the same. The gap between what the market charges and what LifeMiles charges simply grows wider. And then there's the no-fuel-surcharge policy — the detail that separates LifeMiles from competitors like British Airways Avios, which can pile $600+ in carrier surcharges onto a single redemption. With LifeMiles, you pay government taxes only, typically $50–$150 for a transatlantic itinerary. That's it. For the ChooseFI community, this redemption represents exactly the kind of asymmetric value that underpins a great travel rewards strategy: use points where cash prices are highest, eliminate fees wherever possible, and fly a product you'd never justify paying full price for — because you didn't have to.

The core insight here is understanding why Avianca LifeMiles prices Star Alliance awards so aggressively — and then understanding how to get points into the program promptly enough to actually use them.

Sources indicate that avianca is a Star Alliance member, which means it has reciprocal award booking agreements with every other Star Alliance carrier — United, Lufthansa, Swiss, ANA, EVA Air, Singapore Airlines, and more. Like all alliance programs, LifeMiles can sell award seats on partner airlines. The pricing is set by Avianca's own award chart, not by Lufthansa's chart or United's chart.

It has been revealed that this is the pricing inefficiency. Lufthansa's own frequent flyer program (Miles & More) charges over 100,000 miles for the same transatlantic business class route and layers on fuel surcharges. United MileagePlus charges 70,000–88,000 miles for the same seat. Avianca LifeMiles charges 63,000 miles with zero carrier surcharges. Same seat. Same plane. Wildly different cost.

According to recent reports, avianca keeps rates competitive because they want their program to be attractive to non-Avianca flyers — it's a revenue play. And because their route network is South America-focused, they've built a powerful award program that earns loyalty from customers who may never set foot on an Avianca plane.

Many programs claim no surcharges, then quietly pass through "carrier-imposed fees" that look indistinguishable from surcharges. LifeMiles is one of the genuine exceptions. On partner award bookings — including Lufthansa, Swiss, and other carriers that traditionally levy heavy surcharges — LifeMiles charges only government taxes. For a JFK–FRA business class award, expect to pay roughly $50–$150 out of pocket. That's the full cash outlay.

Industry observers note that this is where the transfer partner ecosystem matters. LifeMiles accepts transfers from:.

Industry observers note that the instant Citi transfer is particularly powerful: if you find available award space today, you can move points and call LifeMiles to book within the same session. Capital One and Bilt are nearly as fast. Marriott's 3:1 ratio makes it less efficient unless you have a large Bonvoy balance and no better option.

In a recent development, lifeMiles runs frequent purchased miles sales, often 100%+ bonus miles on purchases. This is a legitimate strategy for topping off your balance when you're a few thousand miles short of a redemption. Combined with transfer partners, it creates significant flexibility. Watch for promotions at lifemiles.com — they typically appear 6–8 times per year.

The golden rule of any points transfer: never transfer miles until you've confirmed award availability. LifeMiles miles are non-refundable once transferred, and award space can disappear in hours.

United MileagePlus has one of the best Star Alliance partner award search tools available to the public. Go to united.com, start a search as if you're booking an award ticket, and look for business class availability on Lufthansa or Swiss flights on your target route. United displays Lufthansa partner space accurately in most cases. You're looking for "saver" level availability — marked as "X" class on Lufthansa.

Recent findings suggest that lufthansa's own website (lufthansa.com) sometimes shows availability that United misses, and vice versa. Search both. You're not booking here — just confirming the seat exists.

Sources indicate that an ExpertFlyer subscription ($10/month) lets you set availability alerts for specific routes and dates. For a high-value redemption like this, it's often worth one month of the service to monitor your target window.

Sources indicate that lifeMiles opens its booking window 355 days in advance. For peak travel periods — summer transatlantic, major European events — set a calendar reminder to search at the 355-day mark. Business class award space on Lufthansa releases in small batches and fills promptly.

Transfer exactly what you need — 63,000 miles for a one-way business class transatlantic award — plus a small buffer of 2,000–3,000 miles for potential routing variations.

Go to lifemiles.com and search your award. The website has improved but can still be inconsistent with partner availability display. If the online search doesn't show the space you found on United.com, call LifeMiles directly at their customer service line. Have your flight numbers, dates, and cabin class ready. Phone agents can access and book partner availability that the website sometimes fails to display.

According to recent reports, after booking, you'll receive a confirmation email with a PNR (record locator). Verify this on the operating carrier's website — go to lufthansa.com or swiss.com and look up your reservation using the PNR. If it pulls up correctly, your booking is solid. Save this confirmation and check it once more 72 hours before departure.

It has been revealed that avianca LifeMiles uses a distance-based award chart for Star Alliance partner flights, and their chart is consistently 15-40% cheaper than competing programs for the same seats. The reason is strategic: Avianca wants to attract members to its loyalty program, and aggressive pricing on aspirational redemptions is how they compete with larger alliances. For you, this means the exact same Lufthansa First Class seat or ANA business class seat costs significantly fewer points when booked through LifeMiles versus through United MileagePlus or the carrier directly. The catch is that LifeMiles availability depends on the operating carrier releasing award space to partners, so you still need to search on the carrier or United.com before transferring.

According to recent reports, card links may earn ChooseFI a commission. See our advertiser disclosure.

Let's walk through a real redemption so you can see exactly what this looks like in practice.

The Route: Fresh York JFK → Frankfurt FRA, nonstop The Aircraft: Lufthansa Boeing 747-8, upper deck business class The Cash Price: $6,500 (a realistic peak-season transatlantic business class fare) The Points Cost: 63,000 Avianca LifeMiles Out-of-Pocket Fees: ~$85 in government taxes CPP Achieved: 10.3 cents per point.

You've transferred 63,000 Citi ThankYou points to LifeMiles — instantly — spotted the award space on United.com the morning it opened, called LifeMiles to confirm, and had your booking locked in within 90 minutes of finding the seat.

Recent findings suggest that lufthansa's 747-8 upper deck business class is one of the most iconic products in commercial aviation. The upper deck seats — in a 2-2-2 configuration — sit quieter and smoother than the main deck, with fewer passengers and a more intimate cabin feel.

Industry observers note that your seat converts to a fully flat bed of approximately 6 feet. You'll have direct aisle access (depending on your seat selection), a large personal entertainment screen, and Lufthansa's catering, which consistently ranks among the top transatlantic carriers. The meal service on JFK–FRA is legitimate: a proper multi-course dinner, a breakfast service as you approach Germany, and a snack menu available throughout.

In a recent development, before you board, you'll have access to Lufthansa's business class lounge at JFK — typically the Lufthansa Business Lounge or, depending on timing, the partner lounge. Hot food, showers, and a genuine departure experience that costs nothing beyond the taxes you've already paid.

The flight itself is roughly 7.5 hours. In a flat bed, that's a real night's sleep — or close enough. You arrive in Frankfurt rested, which matters whether you're connecting onward or starting your trip immediately.

Industry observers note that for the ChooseFI community: this is the redemption that pays for the honeymoon, the milestone anniversary trip, or the family adventure you've been planning since you first discovered travel rewards. The $6,500 you didn't spend stays in your index funds.

In a recent development, book at the 355-day mark for peak dates. Lufthansa releases a small number of partner award seats when the schedule opens. The travelers who get summer business class awards are almost always the ones who searched on day 355. Set a calendar alert. Be ready.

In a recent development, use Citi ThankYou for time-sensitive bookings. Because Citi transfers to LifeMiles are instant, you can find award space and complete your booking in a single session. This matters when you're racing to secure a specific seat before someone else grabs it.

Industry observers note that watch for LifeMiles purchased miles promotions. If you're 10,000–15,000 miles short of a redemption, purchasing miles during a 100% bonus promotion can effectively cost you 0.5–0.7 cents per mile — still leaving you with excellent overall CPP on the redemption. Check lifemiles.com regularly or set a Google Alert for "LifeMiles promotion.".

According to recent reports, verify your booking on the operating carrier's website. After booking through LifeMiles, always look up your PNR on lufthansa.com or swiss.com. If it appears correctly, your seat is real. If it doesn't, call LifeMiles immediately.

Search Swiss as an alternative to Lufthansa. Swiss International Air Lines is also a Star Alliance member, also bookable through LifeMiles at the same rates, and also operates excellent business class products on transatlantic routes. Swiss often has more partner award availability than Lufthansa on certain dates.

In a recent development, never transfer points before confirming availability. This is the most common — and most expensive — mistake in travel rewards. LifeMiles does not allow re-transfers out of the program.

Don't ignore the miles expiry policy. LifeMiles expire 12 months from your last earning activity. Any account activity — earning miles, purchasing miles, even a credit card transaction — resets the clock on your entire balance. Set a recurring reminder every 10 months to run a small transaction if you're holding a balance without an imminent booking.

In a recent development, don't book Lufthansa First Class expecting the same experience. Lufthansa's First Class is a separate product with separate availability and pricing. Business class is the sweet spot here — outstanding value, more seats, and significantly better availability.

Avoid mixing Marriott Bonvoy transfers with tight timelines. At 3:1 and 1–5 days transfer time, Bonvoy is the slowest and least efficient path into LifeMiles. Plan accordingly.

According to recent reports, this redemption is built for the experienced FI traveler who has already earned their first free night or domestic flight and is ready to graduate to aspirational international business class. You don't need to fly business class constantly — but for a honeymoon, a milestone birthday, or a long-planned European trip, this is the redemption that makes the experience extraordinary without derailing your savings rate.

This is NOT the right redemption if:.

You need 63,000 LifeMiles per person, per direction. A couple flying one-way needs 126,000 miles. Most people will get there through a combination of one or two travel credit card welcome bonuses and organic spending — entirely achievable within the FI community's existing card strategy.

## Rated: Hard — Here's Why This redemption earns its **hard** rating from three compounding challenges, none of which is insurmountable but all of which require deliberate effort. **Challenge 1: Award Availability Is Limited.** Lufthansa releases partner award seats conservatively. You may search for weeks before finding space on your preferred route and dates. This isn't a redemption where you decide Tuesday you want to go and book Thursday. You need a booking window of weeks to months, and flexibility in your travel dates helps enormously. **Challenge 2: The Booking Process Has Friction.** LifeMiles' website doesn't always surface partner award availability accurately. You'll likely need to search on United.com to find the space, then call LifeMiles to actually book it. That phone call requires patience — hold times vary, and you'll need to clearly communicate flight numbers, dates, and cabin class to the agent. **Challenge 3: Timing the Transfer Is High-Stakes.** Because you can't transfer points *out* of LifeMiles, you're committing your points the moment you initiate a transfer. Finding the seat, moving the miles, and completing the booking requires confidence and speed. ## How to Overcome the Challenges 1. **Start searching early** — 300+ days out for peak travel. Use ExpertFlyer alerts to monitor availability passively. 2. **Use Citi ThankYou for instant transfers** so you can act immediately when you find a seat. 3. **Practice the phone booking process** once before your high-stakes redemption — call LifeMiles with a simple question to understand their system. If you've successfully booked one or two simpler awards before, you can absolutely do this. The ChooseFI community has members completing this redemption every year — and every single one states the boarding moment made the effort completely worth it.

United demonstrates Star Alliance partner availability that LifeMiles can book. Search for Saver-level awards in business or first class on your target route. Note the exact carrier, flight number, and date.

According to recent reports, amex MR, Chase UR, Citi ThankYou, and Capital One miles all transfer to LifeMiles. Amex transfers are often fastest (same day). Transfer only after confirming availability in Step 2.

According to recent reports, premium cabin award space is limited and competitive. Once your transferred miles appear in your LifeMiles account, complete the booking immediately. Do not wait — the seat can be taken by another searcher.

Industry observers note that lifeMiles charges low taxes and fees on most partner awards, typically $30-$100 depending on the route. Some carriers (notably British Airways) add fuel surcharges, but most Star Alliance carriers keep fees minimal through LifeMiles.

It has been revealed that yes, Lufthansa First Class is bookable through LifeMiles at 87,000 miles one-way from the US to Europe. Availability is limited and typically released at 14 days before departure for partner programs, though some space appears further out. Search on United.com first to confirm Lufthansa First saver space exists before transferring.

Recent findings suggest that transfer times vary by partner. Amex Membership Rewards transfers often post same-day. Chase Ultimate Rewards transfers typically take 1-2 business days. Citi ThankYou and Capital One transfers can take 1-3 days. Always account for transfer time when booking time-sensitive award space.

It has been revealed that most Star Alliance carriers booked through LifeMiles have low or no fuel surcharges. The notable exception is British Airways (a oneworld carrier, not bookable through LifeMiles). Taxes and fees on typical Star Alliance routes run $30-$100 per ticket, making LifeMiles one of the cheapest programs for out-of-pocket award costs.

If the booking fails because award space disappeared between your search and transfer, the miles sit in your LifeMiles account. They do not expire as long as you have account activity every 12 months. You can use them for a future booking, but you cannot transfer them back to your original program.

Industry observers note that this sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

Industry observers note that avianca LifeMiles is the program that lets FI-community travelers fly the same premium cabins as frequent business travelers at a fraction of the points cost. By consistently underpricing Star Alliance awards, LifeMiles turns 63,000-87,000 transferable points into experiences worth $8,000 or more. The process requires discipline (never transfer before confirming availability), patience (searching for saver space takes time), and a willingness to navigate a less polished booking experience. But the value is real: 15-20 cents per point on aspirational flights that would be unreachable at cash prices.

When I became an accredited investor, I found myself among an elite group with the financial means and regulatory clearance to access investments that many couldn’t. This opened doors to exclusive realms like hedge funds, venture capital firms, specific investment funds, private equity funds, and more.

Even though I had this “exclusive access” it took me a while to start investing in alternative asset classes.

The Securities and Exchange Commission states that as an accredited investor, I possess a level of sophistication that equips me to craft a riskier investment portfolio than a non-accredited investor. While this might not be universally true for everyone, in my case, I had demonstrated the financial resilience to bear more risk (see barbell investing), especially if my investments took an unforeseen downturn.

One of the intriguing aspects I discovered was that investment opportunities for accredited investors aren’t mandated to register with financial authorities. This means they often come with fewer disclosures and might not be as transparent as the registered securities available to the general public.

The underlying belief is that my status as a sophisticated investor implies a deeper understanding of financial risks, a need for less disclosure of unregistered securities, and a conviction that these exclusive investment opportunities are apt for my funds.

Industry observers note that on a personal note, as a practicing CFP®, I haven’t always worked with accredited investors. Early in my career, I didn’t quite grasp the allure. However, as time went on, I began to see the broader spectrum of investment options available to accredited investors.

Recent findings suggest that as I learned more the clearer it became why this realm was so sought after. The variety and potential of these exclusive opportunities were truly eye-opening, reshaping my perspective on the world of investing.

It has been revealed that an accredited investor is an individual or a business entity that is allowed to trade securities that may not be registered with financial authorities. They are entitled to this privileged access because they satisfy one or more requirements regarding income, net worth, asset size, governance status, or professional experience.

The concept of an accredited investor originated from the idea that individuals or entities with a higher financial acumen or more resources are better equipped to understand and bear the risks of certain investment opportunities.

Historically, the distinction between accredited and non-accredited investors was established to protect less experienced investors from potentially risky or less transparent investment opportunities.

Regulatory bodies, such as the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), have set criteria to determine who qualifies as an accredited investor, ensuring that they have the financial stability and sophistication to engage in more complex investment ventures.

To be classified as an accredited investor, one must meet specific criteria set by regulatory bodies:.

It has been revealed that the world of accredited investing is dynamic and ever-evolving. Emerging trends suggest a shift towards democratizing investment opportunities, with regulatory bodies considering more inclusive criteria for accredited investor status. This shift aims to balance the need for investor protection with the recognition that financial acumen can come from experience and education, not just wealth.

Sources indicate that furthermore, technological advancements are playing a pivotal role. The rise of blockchain and tokenized assets, for instance, is creating new avenues for investment and might reshape the landscape of opportunities available to accredited investors.

As the line between traditional and alternative investments blurs, the future promises a more integrated, inclusive, and innovative environment for accredited investors.

According to recent reports, understanding the role and opportunities of accredited investors is crucial in the modern financial landscape. While the distinction offers privileged access to unique investment opportunities, it also comes with increased risks and responsibilities.

It has been revealed that as the world of investing continues to evolve, potential accredited investors are encouraged to stay informed, conduct thorough research, and seek professional advice.   • On a $300,000, 30-year fixed loan with 20% down, FICO’s loan savings calculator puts the annual percentage rate, the loan’s yearly cost with fees, at 8.06% for a 660 score and 7.76% for a 720.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that your credit score helps set your mortgage rate, and the fixes that raise it take weeks to show up on your reports, so start three to six months before you apply. Pull all three credit reports, dispute any errors, pay card balances well below their limits before each statement closes, and keep your old cards open.

On a $300,000, 30-year fixed loan with 20% down, FICO’s loan savings calculator puts the annual percentage rate, the loan’s yearly cost with fees, at 8.06% for a 660 score and 7.76% for a 720. Raising your score from 660 to 720 would cut the payment it demonstrates by $63 a month, or more than $22,000 over the life of the loan.

A mortgage lender pulls all three of your credit reports, each with its own score, and usually sets your rate by the middle one. Those scores typically come from older FICO versions mortgage lenders have used for decades, so the free score in your app may not match them. On loans sold to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, lenders can now use another model, VantageScore 4.0, instead.

Either way, an error or a high card balance on any one report can lower your middle score.

In a recent development, pull all three reports at AnnualCreditReport.com, where each is free every week. Dispute any error with each bureau that lists it. A bureau has 30 to 45 days to investigate, so starting six months out leaves time for a second round.

Card issuers usually report each card’s balance on its statement closing date, so pay each balance down well below its limit a few days before the statement closes, not just by the due date.

In a recent development, catch up on any past-due account now, since your score counts how far behind it is today. And keep old cards open, even unused ones. Closing a card removes its limit from your available credit and raises your utilization, the share of that credit your balances use.

A lender sees only what’s on your reports the day it checks your credit, so pull them this week and give each fix time to show up.

To pick the lender you’ll apply with, compare the best mortgage lenders.

  • According to recent reports, lenders base your approval partly on your debt-to-income ratio, the share of your monthly income before taxes that goes to debt payments, figured from the debts you had when you applied.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that once you’re preapproved for a mortgage, hold off on new credit cards, car loans, store financing, and co-signing until after closing. Your lender checks your credit again just before you close, and one new monthly payment can push your debt payments over its limit. That can delay the closing or cancel the loan.

According to recent reports, lenders base your approval partly on your debt-to-income ratio, the share of your monthly income before taxes that goes to debt payments, figured from the debts you had when you applied. Under Fannie Mae’s rules for the loans it buys, lenders must recalculate that ratio whenever upcoming debt turns up, right up to closing day.

Recent findings suggest that in that ratio, every card adds its minimum payment, store cards included. Even a small newly introduced payment can push you past the limit if you were approved close to it, and over the limit, the loan no longer qualifies.

Say a buyer earns $7,500 a month before taxes, her lender caps the ratio at 45%, and she’s approved at 43%. A week before closing, she opens a store card for $4,000 of furniture. Its $160 minimum payment lifts her ratio to 45.1%, and the closing slips two weeks while she pays off the card and the lender reviews the loan again.

Until you close, put these off:.

Recent findings suggest that paying every bill on time stays essential, since a late payment can show up when the lender checks your credit before closing. Comparing several mortgage lenders is still fine. Send every application within about two weeks, and credit scores count them as a single credit check.

Pick out the furniture now, then buy it after closing day with savings rather than a latest store card.
