⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that this post is dedicated to my dear friend Ionatana.
  • Industry observers note that after completing the Auckland section of Te Araroa, Maya and I, headed to Hamilton.
  • So, our recovery continued along the Waikato River.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that this post is dedicated to my dear friend Ionatana. May God’s love, compassion, and mercy fill you, and your family up, then spill over with blessings.

Industry observers note that after completing the Auckland section of Te Araroa, Maya and I, headed to Hamilton. With a week of successful walking down, we felt another week of slack packing is maybe overly cautious, but (in my opinion) necessary. You can never be too careful when walking long distances. Taking care of injuries early, and not rushing through the recovery, is essential.

So, our recovery continued along the Waikato River. This is an established walkway for walkers, bikers, and boat racing watchers. Luckily for us, we managed to pick up this section of trail right as the Bridge 2 Bridge races were happening. Slalom skiers, inflatable speed boats, jet skis, and other raceable water craft wizzed past us as we meandered along the paved path.

In a recent development, the trail, post river, takes you through Hamilton, and deposits you just west of town at the Taitua Arboretum. The weather was a bit stormy this week, so in true hiker fashion, we hunkered down, with our new British friends, at The Bank for the afternoon. We played cards, drank $4 pints, and enjoyed each other’s firm.

Alice and Matt, our fresh favorite British couple.

Sources indicate that feeling fresh, rejuvenated, and healthy, Maya and I set off from the arboretum. Full packs, flexible walking strategy, and high hopes, met by towering native trees, proved a great start to the next leg of our adventure.

The Karamu Walkway is 8.5 km of rolling hills with cool rocks and sheep. Seriously…sheep EVERYWHERE (25,000 to be exactish, according to our friendly trail host). We are just past the lambing season, so all the mama sheep are sheeping about with their lambs. Very cute, except for the fact that all sheep have a severe case of poopy butt, so just don’t look at their rear.

Industry observers note that after our time with the sheep, we experienced our first hut. Picture the AMC’s High Mountain hut system, but a bit smaller, no “Croo”, and the huts are included in our trail pass. Mice…nope. Mattresses…yep. Awesome views and everyone staying there is super friendly…absolutely. The climb up and down the Pirongia Traverse was a true test for Maya’s knee, and she left that stretch feeling tired (of course, it was super muddy!), but energized from how great her legs felt. An overall win, and epic section.

Thank goodness for the board walks as you got closer to the hut.

It has been revealed that sunset with Dr. Seuss tree from the hut deck.

While the sections along the beaches, through farmland, and up and over mountains is why walkers walk, Te Araroa throws some lengthy road walks in there. You know, just to keep you grateful for the time spent not on the road. Walk it, hitch it, whatever. It’s your adventure. Maya and I do put our thumbs out when we can, but if we do end up walking it, we are well prepared with high visibility vests, custom made by Maya herself.

Industry observers note that we are right now in Te Kūiti letting some weather pass and planning our next section which includes bike riding and canoe paddling. Sounds like a fun switch up giving our walking legs a rest, and our biking legs/paddling arms, some strength. Looking ahead appears to be pretty dang fun. Stay tuned to find out.

P.S. I have been carrying a kite, and her maiden voyage was at Putaki Shelter. Her name is Putaki, Taki for short. I tried to fly her again at the Waitomo Top 10 Holiday Park, but the wind had a mind of its own that day. Let’s see how long she last.

Always ready for a good laugh. A long walk, to take the edge off. That challenge you did not want, but are grateful for. And a keeper, of the faith, all the love, and this thing called courage (“soft front, strong back”).

#68068. The Dane Steadman Interview: Hard Going and High Stakes in the Karakoram

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1390 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

The Dane Steadman Interview: Hard Going and High Stakes in the Karakoram

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1390 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There is much more to an expedition than summit or failure.
  • In a recent development, the one factor on the team’s side was the previous experience of Steadman and Cody Winckler.
  • Recent findings suggest that grant Stewart of Canada, the third member of the Sosbun Brakk team, is a skilled climber but was less familiar with the Karakoram.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There is much more to an expedition than summit or failure. In this exclusive interview, American climber Dane Steadman explains why his recent newly introduced route on Karakoram’s Sosbun Brakk (6,414m) “was much more difficult than the one on Yashkuk Sar, both on and off the mountain.” Strong words, considering that he and his partners were awarded a Piolet d’Or for Yashkuk Sar.

In a recent development, the one factor on the team’s side was the previous experience of Steadman and Cody Winckler. “It was our third trip, so we knew a lot more about climbing there,” Steadman noted. Indeed, after Yashkuk Sar, Winckler and Steadman returned to Pakistan in 2025 and climbed two new routes with Blake Berghoff.

Recent findings suggest that grant Stewart of Canada, the third member of the Sosbun Brakk team, is a skilled climber but was less familiar with the Karakoram. His most remarkable climbs had taken place in Alaska and at home in the Canadian Rockies.

Bivy in an ice cave. Photo Dane Steadman.

Comparing the two epic climbs, Steadman highlighted the differences.

“The trip to Yashkuk Sar went incredibly smoothly. Getting there and acclimatizing was great. We had an amazing weather window for the climb. Nothing on it was exceptionally hard, and we did it on the first try, and the descent went without a hitch,” he said.

He explained that the hardest parts of that 2024 first ascent were their lack of experience and the uncertainty that came with it. An unexpected mishap also occurred during the climb itself: a snow mushroom collapsed above them, forcing them to change their ascent route halfway up.

“On the other hand,” Steadman went on, “almost everything about the Sosbun Brakk trip was hard: lost bags, sickness acclimatizing, big storms beforehand and while on the mountain, hard climbing and route-finding, and a very difficult descent through terrible weather.”.

The unclimbed north face of Sosbun Brakk. Photo: Dane Steadman.

Recent findings suggest that “[Overall,] on the Yashkuk trip, I think we felt for most of the time that we would be able to do it with only some moments of doubt here and there,” Steadman admitted. “On Sosbun, we thought much of the time that we wouldn’t be able to do it for all the reasons above. We were quite surprised [to succeed].”.

Recent findings suggest that one unusual aspect of the Sosbun Brakk expedition was its dates. They went to Pakistan and climbed in early fall, two months later than the Karakoram’s typical July-August climbing season. Yet, Steadman says this was planned to account for the changing climate in the high ranges.

In a recent development, approaching the face. Photo: Dane Steadman.

“First, while the Karakoram doesn’t receive as much of the Indian monsoon as the main Himalaya, it is still a monsoonal climate, and I think (and have heard from many locals now) that the weather tends to be much better in the fall than in the summer,” he explained.

“Second, we were concerned about rockfall and generally unsafe conditions on the face, being relatively low and lacking in buttresses. We thought the colder temperatures would make things safer and increase the odds of finding good ice.

“Third, Grant was able to get time off in October more easily than earlier in September. In a perfect world, we probably would have gone one to two weeks earlier, but we worked with what we had.”.

Sources indicate that asked about other expeditions planning to visit the Pakistani mountains in the future, Steadman suggests that October could be a good time for certain climbs, but that September is also great. “This year, the weather was much less stable in September-October than I’ve experienced on my previous trips. Things got much snowier than normal for that time of year, [according to locals], but I think the weather was still better than through most of the summer.”.

The team planned a single alpine-style push in the purest style. However, when they started on the route, they encountered an impassable hanging serac. They had to retreat and decide whether to try a totally different line or go home.

The base camp crew. Photo: Dane Steadman.

The team decided to try a route to the right of the originally planned one. But how could they be sure they wouldn’t reach another dead end?

It has been revealed that steadman admitted it was difficult. “The line we ended up climbing was entirely hidden from view at our base camp and where we acclimatized,” he explained. “[It was] an east-facing gash on a north face, which we only saw from the northwest until we tried it. From all the views we had before the first attempt, the central line we first attempted appeared to be the only route that wouldn’t involve climbing huge walls of monolithic gneiss, as it followed ice streaks and sheets for a good amount of it, and only looked to have relatively short cruxes.

Industry observers note that at the base, they discovered that a tiny but menacing serac hung over the center of the wall, threatening the lower half. (The upper half appeared protected by an overhanging rock wall above it.).

“So we shifted to a different line to the left, which looked much harder but possible, and planned to rejoin our intended line at mid-height, under the protection of the overhangs.

That attempt didn’t so much dead-end as things compounded, forcing a retreat. “We were tired even on the approach from non-stop efforts to get there and acclimatize. We had some equipment complications, were moving slowly, and most of all, the climbing was damn hard,” he remarked.

In the end, they chose to rappel down after a two-hour-plus lead climb on a pitch that hadn’t looked hard from below. Dusk was approaching; there was no bivy spot in sight, and they were only 300m up the 1,800m wall.

Recent findings suggest that “However, from our position on that attempt, we were able to see the right-trending, east-facing gash on the right side of the face, which was totally hidden by monolithic rock walls from all our previous vantage points,” he said. “So, after bailing, we felt like the central line would require fresh bodies, minds, and a huge weather window, but the right-hand line would be much more feasible.”.

Heading up. Photo: Dane Steadman.

The climbers rested for three days in base camp and then set off again. “We certainly felt that we could get shut down at any number of points, especially at the steep mushroom-choked chimney on the headwall below the junction with the northwest spur,” Steadman admitted. “But it seemed like there was a good chance we could do it, and, most importantly, we felt like we could bail from anywhere [if necessary].”.

Sources indicate that the summit ridge of Sosbun Brakk after many tough decisions. Photo: Dane Steadman.

Industry observers note that however, bailing would not be easy. “The lower part would involve rappelling off V-threads, he explained, and if they had to turn back below the headwall, they would need to rappel out right to an icefield.

Industry observers note that route topo: line of ascent in red, line of descent in yellow. Photo: Steadman/Stewart.

Industry observers note that the trio summited on their fifth day on the wall, at 4 pm. Days were now short, and they still had a long, uncertain descent ahead. The descent began on the line of ascent, but eventually deviated to newly introduced terrain.

“We descended the upper half of our route, almost entirely rappelling down the northwest spur, with a little bit of downclimbing/traversing),” Steadman stated.

It has been revealed that they then reached a point west of their ascent line, where the face was slightly smaller and more covered in permanent ice. “Then we rappelled straight down, diagonaling back left partway down to avoid some serac hazard.”.

In a recent development, descending in worsening weather. Photo: Dane Steadman.

Sources indicate that dane Steadman and Cody Winckler of the U.S., together with Grant Stewart of Canada, completed the first ascent of the north face of Sosbun Brakk (6,414m) in Pakistan’s Karakoram last month. The peak had been climbed only once before, by a Japanese team in 1981, from a different, milder side. The new 1,800m route includes difficulties of M7, WI5.

Te Araroa: more muddy boogeymen

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1234 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that in order to walk Te Araroa you must accept mud into your heart (and shoes and socks and blisters).
  • I had been thinking about a zero for about a day and a half before that, but had kept pushing on because I wanted to stay with my group.
  • The dome began with fields of mud, and our group split up pretty early into the day.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that in order to walk Te Araroa you must accept mud into your heart (and shoes and socks and blisters). You also must never trust roots for they are deceivers and false friends (slippery, so slippery). The dome is no exception to these rules. You will never escape the mud until you have completed the trail.

Dome day dawned and I was NERVOUS. I had been thinking about a zero for about a day and a half before that, but had kept pushing on because I wanted to stay with my group. I also made the biggest mistake of my life, not having a coffee.

The dome began with fields of mud, and our group split up pretty early into the day. It was the kind of terrain that we all prefer to navigate solo, it’s no fun when people are watching you slip and slide up and down a muddy hill, or you feel like you’re holding others up. I was feeling so rough mentally, and my hiker hunger had really started to kick in the night before, so I spent the morning mentally cataloguing all the food I had left and whether it would be enough to get me to the dairy in Puhoi. I was exhausted physically and mentally before the day even really began. But I kept going.

Sources indicate that when I told people about walking Te Araroa I talked a lot about wanting to build resilience and the ability to keep going even when I really didn’t want to. Some part of me knew this was the first moment where I could start to learn that. So singing broken clips of songs to myself and sometimes even counting my steps, I trudged on.

I caught up with Sinèad at the end of the first major hill and descent section, and we walked the road section together. I fantasized about going to one of the open houses along the road and asking them for a coffee. I didn’t think they’d let my muddy hiker self in so I kept moving.

When we approached the next significant, forested hill section of the day we found a fellow hiker, Xavier, eating half his lunch. I immediately sat down and ate a handful of every one of my accessible snacks. The others took off and I spent a further ten minutes talking myself into continuing. I knew that on the other side of this hill was a campsite where, if I really wanted to, I could stop for the night. I also knew that in less than a kilometre I’d hit the 500km mark.

Industry observers note that I felt so sleepy, not just tired but burny-eyes-sleepy. I thought desperately about the single sachet of instant coffee deep in my food bag and sang “just keep swimming” to myself. By the time I was about ¾ through this hill I was once again mentally inventorying my meals, trying to decide if maybe I could break this section into two days.

In a recent development, then I heard some girls ahead of me and like a puppy seeing its people again after a long work day, I perked up, thinking it was my friends. Unfortunately it was just two very clean-looking, white-sneakered day hikers.

Recent findings suggest that though they weren’t who I was hoping to see, the whiteness of their sneakers told me that from here, the trail would be more chill. I pushed on and eventually I could hear Sinèad’s accent floating through the trees. And there was our friend, Zoe, getting water from the stream! I crossed the stream and climbed up to the campground where I was delighted to find there was a picnic table so I wouldn’t have to sit on the ground.

Sources indicate that I laid out my very wet tent to dry (still thinking about staying there), drank the last of my water, and filtered some into my mayo-turned cold soak jar to shake up my last instant coffee sachet. Sinèad stated she watched me essentially reboot as soon as I started drinking the coffee.

This was when the trail got easier.

It was 1:30 at this point, we’d been walking for six and a half hours, and I didn’t really have a sense of how much further there was to go. I decided to take a long lunch and to eat two wraps, food inventory be damned!

And then my saviours began to arrive. First was another set of day hikers, the older of whom helpfully told me I seemed very tired (I did not hold back when I agreed with him). And then Annabel, who I had been worried about because she normally walks at a similar pace to me and I hadn’t seen her all day.

After some lecturing about my choice to not wear boots, the day hikers gave me a bag of pumpkin seeds, dates and ANZAC biscuits. The snacks were enough to convince me to put my wet, muddy socks back on and walk the final five or six kilometres to the dome cafe.

Annabel and I climbed the third and final hill of the day which was actually suddenly easy terrain, and then descended a really well-graded, touristy track. I honestly felt like I was flying on that terrain and having Annabel around to chat to made it go really quickly. After eleven hours of walking (including the two hour lunch I took) we made it to camp. The dome cafe was an oasis, it had a bathtub and yes I did sit down in it. I pitched my tent and we all took turns having a hot shower and I think that place saved my life. My mashed potatoes have never tasted better. This was a big day of learning for me. Mostly that I can do it even when it’s a tough day.

I hope my work colleagues enjoy seeing my muddy sock water.

In a recent development, anchor me by The Mutton Birds. It should be noted that I did not choose this. It was unceremoniously bestowed upon me by the “here’s a song you didn’t want stuck in your head” gods. But it would be disingenuous to choose anything else because it is what was mostly going through my mind when I wasn’t inventorying my food or dreaming of coffee.

Now I spend my time convincing my friends to do big walks with me and taking on overly-ambitious craft projects. This season I'm attempting a thru-hike of Te Araroa, starting October 2026.

#68066. Natural Wonders: Crowley Lake Columns

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1054 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Natural Wonders: Crowley Lake Columns

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1054 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that it is low tide on Crowley Lake in Mono County, California.
  • Crowley Lake is a man-made reservoir, administered by the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power.
  • Father Crowley made it his mission to bolster tourism in the area.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that it is low tide on Crowley Lake in Mono County, California. The water is still, the trout abundant, and one or two kayakers paddle about, enjoying the lack of tourists. But as you walk along the shore, something out of place appears: spiral pillars and arches that seem left over from some ancient civilization.

Crowley Lake is a man-made reservoir, administered by the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power. It was named after an important figure in the community, affectionately known as the Desert Padre. This beloved Catholic priest worked tirelessly to help a community that experienced water shortages throughout the 1920s and 1930s. Water from the nearby Owen Valley was diverted to Los Angeles, leaving very little for local residents.

Father Crowley made it his mission to bolster tourism in the area. The publicity led authorities to help locals by drawing up plans for a dam and reservoir. When Father Crowley died in a car accident, authorities completed the Long Valley Dam and named the reservoir Lake Crowley. If it weren’t for his intervention, the lake wouldn’t have existed.

As the years passed, visitors continued coming to Lake Crowley to fish, kayak, camp, and hike. Then something weird started to appear on the cliffsides. The banks appeared to be receding and hollowing out, revealing hundreds upon hundreds of spiral columns. Many onlookers believed they were man-made. Some compared the formations to Moorish architecture from North Africa and Spain.

Though the reservoir is man-made, the area’s history dates back millennia. Crowley Lake lies in the wider Long Valley Caldera, one of Earth’s largest calderas.

According to recent reports, some of the columns. Photo: Shutterstock.

Industry observers note that the caldera sits atop one of three ancient supervolcanoes in the United States. Around 760,000 years ago, this supervolcano erupted and spewed 650 cubic kilometers of rhyolite rock and ash into the air for a week. It covered the land in a blanket of ash and debris over one kilometer thick. And it left behind a 32km long, 18km wide, and 900m deep depression in the earth.

The depression formed when the subterranean magma chamber emptied onto the surface and the remnant shell of a roof collapsed. The blast and pyroclastic flow were so powerful that ash fell as far as Kansas. Along the rim are the lava dome complexes of Mammoth, Glass, and Bald Mountains. The caldera also hosts a cluster of hydrothermally active lakes called the Mammoth Lakes.

The main feature left by the eruption is the Bishop Tuff, a few square kilometers in area. A tuff is a rock of compacted volcanic ash. At the base of this tuff stand the Crowley Lake Columns. They range in thickness, average about six meters high, and are generally reddish, beige, grey, or white with a dark water line at their base. Some lean while others stand straight.

In a recent development, attached by arches, the columns are so evenly spaced that to some visitors, it resembles an ancient temple. Horizontal cracks about 30cm apart add further detail to the columns. They look like they hold up the cliffs but they simply remained after the softer cliff rock started to erode.

The high levels of silica, sodium, and potassium in the columns make the rock conduct heat well and cool suddenly. This led to the cracks. Similar formations exist in Guatemala, Mexico, and New Mexico.

Sources indicate that the few people who frequent Crowley Lake have long known about the columns. Only recently, social media has started to highlight them. This is due to its seclusion on the lake’s shoreline. The only ways to access them are on foot or by boat, kayak, or 4×4. The dirt road on which you turn from Highway 395 is so steep and uneven that it can bog down vehicle. Visitors tend to drive halfway, then walk.

Despite popular speculation that these columns are an example of columnar jointing, they are not. The geological process is different. With columnar jointing, the spaces are not so far apart. A study by geologists at UC Berkeley used a combination of computer models, X-ray diffraction, and electron microscope imagery to determine how they formed. It turns out that the culprit is simply…water.

“We hypothesize that the columns are a result of instabilities at the liquid water and steam interface as cold water seeped into the still-cooling Bishop Tuff,” says Noah Randolph-Flagg, the study’s lead scientist.

The columns formed through hydrothermal convection. Photo: Shutterstock.

It has been revealed that essentially, rainwater seeped down into the hot ash and started to boil, producing a mineral glue called mordonite. The boiling water formed a column of steam which carried the mordonite upward through the rock. Thus, the mineral hardened the rock, leading it to remain standing while the surrounding rock eroded. This process is called hydrothermal convection or circulation.

According to recent reports, according to Randolph-Flagg, it only took 100 years to form these columns. The study also states that “the liquid water–steam interface probably is the source of the instability that generates columnar flow.”.

It has been revealed that as for the erosion of the cliffside, the reservoir’s water levels fluctuate throughout the year with the seasons. After the completion of the reservoir, the columns started to reveal themselves. The constant rise and fall as well as a repeating freeze-thaw cycle caused the tuff to recede. It revealed the columns and also hollowed out the cliffside to form shallow caves. Take care when going into these little caves or pushing on the columns, as they might not be as stable. As the cliff continues to erode, we should see more of these columns.

The arches resemble Moorish architecture. Photo: Shutterstock.

Recent findings suggest that in terms of the Long Valley Caldera, scientists have closely monitored its activity, which has been increasing since the 1980s. Since it is a one of only 20 supervolcanoes in the world, they have paid close attention to its potential for eruption, despite its status as inactive.

There have been small earthquakes and signs of movement in the earth as if it were “breathing.” This is seen in Yellowstone, another supervolcano. While there are no immediate signs of an impending eruption, the caldera’s history and current activity suggest that it is possible.

#68062. Everest Winds Force Climbers to Retreat

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (515 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Everest Winds Force Climbers to Retreat

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (515 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that despite weather forecasts of high winds on Everest, the Russian team gamely left for the West Shoulder today.
  • According to recent reports, “It’s calm right now, but the forecast is worrying,” leader Andrei Vasiliev wrote yesterday from a snow cave, where Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and Vasiliev had sheltered for the night at 6,400m.
  • The three climbers had fixed three pitches above them, according to Mountain Club, and were hoping for firmer terrain as they approached the West Shoulder of Everest, en route to the West Ridge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that despite weather forecasts of high winds on Everest, the Russian team gamely left for the West Shoulder today. But in the end, they couldn’t fight the gale-force winds, which eventually forced them back to their tent at the base of the mountain.

According to recent reports, “It’s calm right now, but the forecast is worrying,” leader Andrei Vasiliev wrote yesterday from a snow cave, where Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and Vasiliev had sheltered for the night at 6,400m. Late today, they confirmed that the weather forecast of powerful winds was unfortunately right.

The three climbers had fixed three pitches above them, according to Mountain Club, and were hoping for firmer terrain as they approached the West Shoulder of Everest, en route to the West Ridge.

However, as we previously reported after consulting meteorologist Vitor Baia of Portugal, conditions were good Tuesday and Wednesday, but winds rose dramatically today.

It has been revealed that on a previous foray up Everest, one of the climbers heads for the West Shoulder. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

“The winds are very strong,” Vasiliev reported. “It is impossible to work higher on the mountain.”.

It has been revealed that vasiliev said that his team is retreating to a tent at 5,600m. This is below the Lho La Pass, possibly on the Khumbu Glacier beside the vertical section leading to that col.

The question is whether the team will wait there for better conditions, retreat to their base in Lobuche, or call off the expedition.

Some charts still show a chance of variable winds tomorrow, before the jet stream hits the mountain with full force (see below).

Wind levels at around summit altitude on Everest this week, by meteoexploration.com.

Baia indicates the winds will remain high every day until next Tuesday. From Wednesday on, the winds should be weaker.

The Russians set off on their third trip up Everest last Monday, hoping to summit via the West Ridge without oxygen or external support, and with no one else on the mountain.

Sources indicate that on Tuesday evening, they checked in with Mountain Club from their tent at 6,000m, where they spent the night. The hard trailbreaking through fresh snow had slowed their pace, but they expected better conditions on the following day, as they started up steeper terrain toward Everest’s shoulder. They knew the snow up there was harder and compacted. They could even see their trails from the previous trip up, so no latest soft snow had accumulated.

Industry observers note that the Russian team on Everest’s West Shoulder. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

Yesterday, Vasiliev noted that they had climbed four pitches on old fixed ropes, plus another eight pitches of their own. The team is fixing ropes at the hardest sections, but not entirely along the route. As expected, snow conditions had improved with the more vertical terrain, but as Vasiliev pointed out, “it’s not exactly easy walking yet.”.

The Russian leader insists the route to the summit is doable. However, wind delays and a lack of time may ultimately end their attempt.

#68061. Breaking: Yosemite At Last! — John Muir Trail Day 21

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2599 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Yosemite At Last! — John Muir Trail Day 21

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2599 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It continued to rain for a while, off and on, and the wind came up again, continuing throughout the night.
  • In a recent development, on one of those, in the middle of the night, I did something clever.
  • Above all, I worried about what I would be facing in the morning.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Total Elevation Gain:  46,975 feet.

Pace (minutes per mile):  28:21.

It was a fitful, fretful night. It continued to rain for a while, off and on, and the wind came up again, continuing throughout the night. The whole time I was worrying about staying warm, staying dry, and making the fewest possible excursions outside to pee.

In a recent development, on one of those, in the middle of the night, I did something clever. I picked up my poncho, which was just lying on the ground soaking wet, and I draped it over a pine tree, so it looked like a scarecrow. Or maybe a scare-bear?

Above all, I worried about what I would be facing in the morning.

Industry observers note that indeed, the morning came. I got up reasonably early, at 6:30, and had breakfast in my tent. In my warm, now semi-dry tent.

Recent findings suggest that the good thing was that the rain had stopped. The poncho I stood up as a decoy in the night, was now wind dried. So, I used it for staging. I put it on the wet ground and pulled all of my stuff out of the tent and placed it on the dry poncho. If things were dry, they stayed dry; if wet, at least they didn’t get any wetter.

Things looked a LOT better at my camp site in the morning!

This mattered, because I had a lot of wet stuff. I had a wet hoodie. I had wet shorts, wet socks, and wet shoes.

Sources indicate that after evacuating the tent, I took it down. Thanks to the wind, the fly – that had been soaking wet — was basically dry. But the ground cloth and the bottom of the tent were very wet.

According to recent reports, what to do? I could either dry them and be done with it, or pack them wet, and dry them later. While thinking about this, I put them on logs, and laid them out to dry, so that my indecision became a decision. When the sun peeked out a little, I put them on rocks. Yes, it ate up a lot of time, but when they were finally dry, I could stop worrying about that issue and just hike.

At 9:00 a.m. I set off. I was wearing wet-cold shoes, wet-cold shorts, wet-cold gloves, a wet-cold hoodie, and a wet-cold hat. Only one thing was not wet and cold:  I decided to go ahead and use my dry socks. I hoped that my shoes were just moist and not soaking wet, and my dry socks would be a barrier to that moisture. That plan worked out pretty well.

Because it was cold in the aftermath of the storm, I started with a lot of energy, to get my blood flowing. I needed it too, for the trail sang one refrain:  up, up, up, and up.

Looking back at the hill I climbed — but at least I was warm, and getting dry!

Sources indicate that by the time I reached the ridge, and looked down on Garnet Lake, I was mostly dry and all warmed up. Then I got lost.

I could see Garnet Lake, I just couldn’t see how to GET there!

According to recent reports, I knew I had to go east, and I spotted a little trail to the east, so I started down that trail until it kind of disappeared. Then I spent about ten minutes wandering around up there, trying to find my way, unable to believe the east-going trail was a false trail. Finally, I retraced my steps far enough to notice a separate west-going trail. That was counterintuitive, but it was the correct trail, because it eventually looped around, lower down, and went east, as I knew it should.

I name this “One Pine Tree Island” in Garnet Lake.

According to recent reports, walking along the shore of Garnet Lake I envisioned what might have happened if I had made it to this destination in the storm the day before. I could imagine myself, struggling with my tent in the rain, and having a huge gust of wind lift the tent like a beach ball and deposit it in the middle of the lake! It would have been bad! Yes, hilarious, but bad.

To reinforce the power of the storm the day before, this was Ninja Queen’s  description of her experience, as she sent it to me via text, with almost no editing:.

“…you can imagine how horribly wrong the day of the storm went for me. I should have hunkered down early like most other hikers had, but I foolishly trusted my (Garmin) InReach weather forecast a little too much, went over Island Pass (a tiny pass but a pass nonetheless) when the storm hit full force two hours early. It was bad. Really, really bad. The trail flooded very rapidly, got washed out and started diverging in multiple directions from the torrential downpour. They were ankle-deep and I kept losing the actual trail; it had become mini rivers at that point. Needless to say, I got wetted out through and through, shivering intensely, my hands no longer functioning, unable to take another step. I ended up setting up camp on some random flat-ish spot over some vegetation that also started pooling water. I was so afraid my tent was going to get flooded. Almost everything inside the tent was wet and muddy as well, though I was able to change into dry sleep clothes and sleeping bag, thanks to my nylofume pack liners. It took me a couple of hours, but I eventually warmed up in the bag, cooked and ate food inside (bears were the last of my worries at this point) and drank as little water as possible so I wouldn’t have to go out until the next morning. Putting back on cold, dripping wet clothes the next morning felt torture-adjacent; something I hope I’ll never have to go through again.”.

“It gave me a small chuckle seeing other hikers also emerge from non-established tent sites the next morning. I quickly learned what I went through was not a typical rainstorm experience. Almost everyone I talked to remarked it had been one of the worst storms they’ve seen on trail. One guy, a firefighter, told me this was far worse than the hurricane weather he had caught on the AT (Appalachian Trail) a few years back. Now I felt like a survivor, instead of feeling like a fair weather backpacker who crumbled at the slightest hint of bad weather.”.

I filled up my water at the bridge where a stream exits the lake. There were a lot of folks around there, laying out their tents to dry from the storm. It was surprising, and a little disturbing, to see how much foam, and even spume-like foam, was on Garnet Lake, which looks otherwise pristine. I didn’t ask anybody about it at the time, who would I ask?

But later I Googled AI and discovered:  “…foam usually forms naturally when decaying plants, algae, and organic debris release compounds that lower water surface tension, and wind or wave action whips air into bubbles.”  In other words, the wind from the storm had produced the foam, not some giant industrial complex just out of view!

I continued up, from Garnet to beautiful Ruby Lake, then to Emerald Lake, and finally the Thousand Islands Lake. This was an exceptionally scenic stretch.

I think this was Ruby Lake… if the water were sparkling red, it would be easier to tell!

Of course this was Thousand Islands Lake — with a pretty terrific backdrop!

According to recent reports, there was very little elevation gain from there to Island Pass. Once the trail reached the ridge on the opposite side of the lake it seemed to stay at a mostly constant elevation for a very long time. The longer it went on, the more I wondered, “Pass? Is there really a pass up here somewhere? Where?”.

No pass, but a pretty cool-looking mushroom!

In a recent development, how can you tell when you have reached a pass? When you can see the other side of the mountain. It felt like that was never going to happen.

Finally, it was getting to be lunchtime. I decided to sit next to a charming little pond up there, and to eat my lunch.

Basically, I ate half of the food that I had brought as lunch, saving the other half for “second lunch.”  But afterwards, I just didn’t feel like I had much energy. Even finally reaching the edge did not inspire me. I saw the edge of the pass and started heading down, but my legs felt heavy. My legs felt like limp spaghetti.

When your legs don’t want to go, you need your brain to execute an override. So, I forced myself to keep going. Finally, I stopped again and made myself a second lunch in that sort of halfway space between Island Pass and Donohue Pass. About five miles separated them and Donohue represented the entrance to Yosemite National Park.

A dead tree by a stream; dead is how I felt before second lunch!

After lunch I had more energy, and I continued.

Throughout the JMT, whenever I approached a location where I knew there was a pass in the ridgeline, I always looked up to see if I could figure out where it might be. “Is that it? No, is that it? Wait, is that it?”  I suspect most hikers do this.

According to recent reports, with Donohue Pass it was hidden around the corner of an extending hump of rock, so of course I guessed wrong. Just short of the summit, I saw a full backpack about 25 yards from the trail. That seemed strange and I looked around. Was someone off going to the bathroom? There was nothing but silence. I continued on, but with a nagging worry for whoever was not connected with their pack.

According to recent reports, when I arrived on top, at 11,066 feet elevation, I was all alone. In honor of my son Gabriel, who coined the pun, I bellowed, “YO! SEMITE!!!”  I got no answer, not even an echo. Even so, I was in Yosemite. It felt strange to be just a few days from the end — barring injury, of course.

As I headed down from Donohue, I thought, “On the one hand, I don’t want to set up in the dark. But there are not too many campsites up here and, of course, I am a couple of miles behind schedule because of the storm.”  I resolved to take a chance and push it a little bit.

As a result, the riverside campsites just below Donohue Pass did not tempt me; they were filling up in any case.

The first camp north of Donohue Pass was by this ugly little lake….

According to recent reports, instead, I descended rapidly and with determination. As I did, I encountered a group heading southbound, up to the pass behind me. One young man was not carrying a pack. Apparently, he had come down to assist his family in making the ascent. He told me, “I left my pack up near the Pass so that I would not be encumbered in helping my family.”  I breathed deeply; mystery solved.

Recent findings suggest that the first stretch went through rocky scree. I asked the mountain gods, “Why is there so much rocky scree?”  They rewarded me with forest.

It has been revealed that see the meadow, far below there? My campsite was somewhere down there….

The descent continued sharply through the woods, and I passed several gorgeous camping sites near the steeply dropping steam. Each time I told myself, “No! Not yet!” and then each time I regretted it, and wondered if I would ever find another spot, after that perfect one I had just rejected.

At last, the steep downhill tapered off, and I reached the valley at the bottom. The stream, now wider and larger, and the trail continued to parallel each other. The going became easier for both the water and my legs.

Following the river there were a few more possible places. As the sun slipped behind the mountains, but still with plenty of light, I saw a knoll overlooking a wide meadow. On that knoll was a lovely camping spot. I was home for the night.

The sun remains on the hillside, even as it gets dark in the valley.

My dinner was rice and beans and chicken, Santa Fe style. I let it soak as I pitched my tent and arranged my site. I let it soak some more as I explored higher up, in the giant granite boulders above the site, to find a cat hole location. It soaked still longer as I dug the hole in preparation for the next morning. But then, with no chores left to do, I got impatient. I ate.

According to recent reports, the dish was very well-seasoned, very tasty. This was certainly a meal I would recommend having again, on another hike, in another place. But rice takes a long time to absorb water when cold-soaking, and I didn’t wait long enough. The flavors were great, but the rice was… crunchy. I didn’t care much. It had been a strenuous day, coming the day after the intense storm. I was tired and hungry and starved for calories. I ate it all with gusto, crunch and all!

Sources indicate that I was feeling good. It was a long day, and I had crossed two passes. I was finally in Yosemite. I haven’t mentioned the aftermath of my fall too much in recent posts, but my ribs were finally hurting less. My wrist was still a problem, to some degree, but it was functional.

Sources indicate that the next day, I would be passing through Tuolumne Meadow. There I would either get a permit for Half Dome, or I would not. If I did, I probably had three days of hiking left. If I did not, then it would likely be two days. I had well under forty miles to go.

As the twilight deepened, I was loving my campsite facing the open meadow. I was proud of the mileage I had achieved, after the shortened day in the storm. My eyes closed and I welcomed blissful sleep.

#68059. Breaking: Piolet d'Or Team Shares Insider Tips for Climbing in Peru's Huayhuash Range

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1293 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Piolet d'Or Team Shares Insider Tips for Climbing in Peru's Huayhuash Range

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1293 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that marc Toralles, Ruben Sanmartin, and Bru Busom of Spain were awarded a Piolet d’Or for a highly committing new route on Yerupaja Grande (6,634m), the highest peak of Peru’s Huayhuash range.
  • Industry observers note that in the last few years, the Andes have reportedly been affected by climate change.
  • “That means that climbers need to pick their route carefully [when judging] what lingers above them,” Buson explained.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that marc Toralles, Ruben Sanmartin, and Bru Busom of Spain were awarded a Piolet d’Or for a highly committing new route on Yerupaja Grande (6,634m), the highest peak of Peru’s Huayhuash range. ExplorersWeb asked the young climbers about the ascent and the unique character of the Andes. They offered some tips for climbers looking to add Peru to their list of high-altitude destinations.

Industry observers note that in the last few years, the Andes have reportedly been affected by climate change. “The main effect is that the huge snow structures on the summits are exposed to warmer temperatures and become more fragile,” Sanmartin said. “Basically, they fall down more easily.”.

“That means that climbers need to pick their route carefully [when judging] what lingers above them,” Buson explained.

In a recent development, bru Buson, left, and Marc Toralles. Photo: Ruben Sanmartin.

This was especially noticeable last year on Siula Grande. “There was a snowfield midway up the face as we trekked by, and on our way back, it was not there anymore,” said Marc Toralles. “Somehow, the melting process in the Andes, with its 5,000m and even 6,000m [altitudes], is similar to what we are seeing every year in the Alps, where we all work as mountain guides.”.

According to recent reports, for Toralles, the best thing in the Andes is how accessible the mountains are. “It’s so easy to go climbing there,” he remarked.

Recent findings suggest that there are no lifts or paved roads, but you can go, climb a peak, and return in three or four days. Something like that in the Himalaya would take weeks. All you need is to get to Huaraz by plane, bus, or car from Lima, where you may stay some days to acclimatize (there are many options), and then go to the mountains.

According to recent reports, if your planned peak is not in the right conditions, you will surely find some other one to climb. Also, the options are infinite for ice climbing, alpine climbing, rock, trekking, anything.

Recent findings suggest that the team’s base camp. Photo: Spanish Yerupaja Grande team.

Recent findings suggest that red tape is minimal. There are no permits for peaks. Instead, climbers and trekkers pay a small fee to cross the comunidades (the areas) where they want to climb, and climbers can hire arrieros (riders with mules) to help carry equipment and supplies to base camps or higher. On this occasion, the climbers kept their logistics basic, with little beyond a slightly larger base camp tent.

With some of the more accessible places, it is advisable to have someone watching over your base camp while you are away climbing.

Once you leave the beaten track, you’ll be alone. “There are no crowds in Huayhuash,” Buson mentioned. Why aren’t they more popular? The climbers explained that Huayhuash peaks are typically more difficult than popular options in the Cordillera Blanca, also in Peru. But they note this lack of popularity is changing fast. “We are seeing much more people in recent years, both climbing and trekking,” they said.

Thanks to the many possibilities, the three Spanish climbers didn’t need to do much planning. “We know Huayhuash pretty well, we are familiar with the terrain and the climbing style, and we are aware there are always options,” said Toralles, who has climbed there four times.

That said, the line the Spaniards climbed on Yerupaja last year was not improvised. They had that route in their mind for some time. “We heard of someone who had tried but called the attempt off, so the route was there to be climbed,” Toralles said. “In addition, it didn’t require a long time, and the timing worked for me, since I was traveling to Peru anyway to do some guiding.”.

Buson and Sanmartin joined immediately. To acclimatize, they had worked double shifts the previous weeks around Chamonix, where both are professional guides. “Working on the Mont Blanc massif intensively was great training and acclimatization,” they said. “We were ready by the time we set foot on the mountain.”.

The best time to climb in Huayhuash is July, August, and the first half of September.

Once on the mountain, they carefully checked the conditions of the face and the line they would follow. “In the Andes, you have to assume that the summit ridge snow formations, the famous ‘mushrooms,’ the significant cornices, and the seracs on the sides of the face are mostly in a delicate state. You need to assume that you will progress on deep, unstable snow, and the entire structure may have deteriorated and be prone to crumble,” Buson noted.

According to recent reports, to deal with them, the climbers used some custom-made tools: They attached alitas (little wings) to their ice axes for a better grip on foamy, loose snow. They also carried small snowshoes for some sections.

According to recent reports, ice axe with ‘alitas’ (wings). Photo: Nick Sheldon/Mountain Project.

According to recent reports, conditions in the Andean mountains are always variable. “You’ll find different terrain depending on the altitude and the orientation,” Sanmartin added. “This is why technical routes on these peaks require a high level of commitment, which, as happened on our route, may be even higher than the intrinsic difficulty of the pitches,” Toralles explained.

With this in mind, the Spanish team named the route they opened Essence of Commitment.

In a recent development, marc Toralles ready for the ridge, with large snow pickets and an ice axe with ‘wings’ attached. Photo: Buson/Sanmartin.

In this sort of terrain, it is paramount to stay focused and make the right call between subjective and objective factors. “There are countless reasons to turn around on climbs like this, but one must keep going, except for obvious reasons, such as an injury, a completely impassable section, or a really violent storm,” Sanmartin remarked.

“That is why it is important to consider all options and potential issues before starting the climb. You need to be sure you like the line and want to climb it.”.

In a recent development, asked whether they reached a point of no return during their climb, Buson admitted they did. “On reaching the ridge, we became aware that trying to downclimb the same route would be quite complex. However, we also saw the route upward was doable.”.

Sources indicate that the Spaniards did not count on a professional meteorologist. “We had our friends texting us the online, free forecasts over InReach,” they noted. “One of the positive aspects of Huayhuash is that good weather periods tend to last for quite a while. Weather windows of five to six days are common.” During their climb, for example, they enjoyed acceptable weather, with some rain and snow but no high winds.

They warn that conditions in the Andes are changing quickly. “You need to observe the mountains and adapt,” Toralles said. “Some people aim for a route based on the information in a guidebook printed 50 years ago, and find a totally different scenario.” He pointed out that Siula Grande looked different in 2025 than it did when he climbed it just three years earlier.

Industry observers note that sanmartin noted that conditions have also changed on normal routes. They are now drier, more complex, and often more hazardous. “In some cases, climbers are abandoning the normal routes up the glaciers and opt for ridges which may be more difficult but in better conditions,” he mentioned.

The climbers think the Andes will not get as crowded as the Himalaya, simply because the logistics are not as advanced — no refuges, no helicopters — and because they don’t have the sizzle of being the tallest peaks on Earth. “But they have incredible potential,” they said.

#68056. The Long Rainy Road

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1256 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

The Long Rainy Road

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1256 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that I have had extraordinary luck to largely avoid precipitation for many weeks.
  • Any hope of escaping with a dry tent vanished in the early morning hours.
  • Recent findings suggest that A little drizzle began to fall intermittently as I made my way along the rocky trail back to Pulpit Rock.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that I have had extraordinary luck to largely avoid precipitation for many weeks. That is about to change.

Any hope of escaping with a dry tent vanished in the early morning hours. The first domino to fall. Now I had to hope that it wouldn’t be actively raining when it comes time to pack up camp. It promptly becomes impossible to keep my pack dry in such a scenario, how do I keep the pack dry when I have to disassemble and roll up my only dry place? Lucky for me, when light first broke the rain noise had stopped. I patted the walls of my tent to dispel some of the leftover water and checked the time. 6:17AM. I decided to save breakfast for later and go straight into packing up so I could check the sunrise and then get to hiking before the precipitation inevitably arrived. At The Pinnacle my instincts were correct, nothing but a small patch of orange glow that could have been a candy wrapper blowing in the wind. I was unbothered, any day where there is rain but I don’t have to pack up in the rain is alright with me. With rain imminent I chose to throw on my poncho, though that decision was partially based on the chillier than expected morning and early start time.

Recent findings suggest that A little drizzle began to fall intermittently as I made my way along the rocky trail back to Pulpit Rock. Conveniently, I can save a few rocky steps by taking the clear driveway past the the Lehigh Valley Amateur Astronomical Society observatories. Its worth mentioning that the society provides a privy and trash can that can be used by hikers. They do ask that hikers don’t camp on the property or use flashlights, for obvious reasons. At the far end of the site I arrived at Pulpit Rock, which still offered a nice view despite the cloudy skies.

From there I didn’t hesitate to use the road down from the observatories all the way down to the Windsor Furnace Shelter. I had a quick breakfast and got back on trail before 8:30AM. Hardly any rain had fallen, I wondered if I’d again be getting lucky with the weather and get all the way back to my van without getting soaked. I pushed hard to get the 5 or so miles to Port Clinton done. I knew the steep leafy trail awaited me and I was holding my breathe to get through that section before any heavy rain arrived – it would not be fun going up that section if the trail was steep, leafy, and turning into a stream all at the same time.

Recent findings suggest that remarkably, the rain continued to hold off. I got closer and closer to Port Clinton, slowly realizing that the 60% chance of rain I saw for nearly every hour the day was landing in the 40% zone at least to start the day. I made it down the trail into town, back across the Schuykill River, and through the train yard. I charged up the hill, still expecting rain at any moment. The climb up proved tough, but not as treacherous as the climb down. This is the one time working against gravity actually works with you. Soon I was back on the ridge and heading toward the gravel road that would take me all the way back to my van on route 183. I thought that if the rain fell there it wouldn’t be a big deal, the hiking would at least be easy.

The Lehigh Valley Amateur Astronomical Society observatories near Pulpit Rock.

Breakfast at the Windsor Furnace Shelter.

A steep climb coming out of the Windsor Furnace Shelter.

I was just starting to think of the impossible. Could I get all the way back to my van without any serious rain? It would take about 3 and half hours to get all the way back to my van hiking at full bore on the gravel road. I didn’t have any stops to make, I was in a straight race with nature. My hopes slowly grew and then, with a single sound, were completely erased. On a downhill section of the road I heard thunder ahead. The forecast didn’t say anything about thunderstorms, but I suppose it didn’t say it would be dry for the better part of the morning either. I was fairly exposed on the road, there was going to be rain, and soon it came. I pulled my poncho back over me, I had stashed it over my shoulders during the climb to stay cool, staying dry was the priority now.

The wind blew and the rain progressed quickly from light drizzle to a steady downpour. The thunder bellowed louder and I began seeing flashes of lightning. The the rain started to feel sharp on my exposed hands. My gloves aren’t waterproof so it isn’t really worth it wear them in the rain. The rain had become freezing rain. Then it became hail the size of Nerds candy. The hail only lasted a few minutes, but the rain continued on. Although the day was in the mid 40s, the rain was ice cold. As soon as the rain became heavy my shoes and socks flooded. All I could do was shake my head and laugh, I had finally run out of luck, and things were regressing to the mean, emphasis on mean.

Sources indicate that none of the surprisingly severe weather slowed me down. I was determined to get back to my van and get dry. The rain continued for almost 2 hours. When it did finally stop, I noticed that the water drops on the trees appeared frozen in place. It looked like ice hanging on the branches and made it look a lot like I was hiking on a rainy, cold winter afternoon. For good, measure, the sun decided to come out with about 30 minutes left. A nice thought, but it was going to take more than a few rays of sunlight to dry out my shoes.

Walking the gravel road just before the weather arrived.

Walking the gravel road just before the weather arrived.

It’s hard to see in the picture, but the scene had gotten considerably more wintery.

Near the end of the hike, the sun comes out.

Total: 24.4 miles, 45,270 steps.

Lucky Skier Survives Night in Crevasse With Two Broken Legs

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, thirty-nine-year-old Emeric Ossatte was ski touring alone earlier this week in the Savoie area of the French Alps, near the Italian border.
  • Industry observers note that the Grenoble-area man, who wasn’t carrying a beacon or radio, doffed his backpack and crawled 100m through the crevasse, looking for a way out.
  • In a recent development, according to a Facebook report by France’s CRS Savoie mountain-rescue unit, they saw the slide path but no immediate sign of Ossatte.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, thirty-nine-year-old Emeric Ossatte was ski touring alone earlier this week in the Savoie area of the French Alps, near the Italian border. He removed his skis to posthole up a steep couloir in his boots and crampons when an avalanche swept him downhill, depositing him into a crevasse and breaking both his legs.

Industry observers note that the Grenoble-area man, who wasn’t carrying a beacon or radio, doffed his backpack and crawled 100m through the crevasse, looking for a way out. But the sides of the crack were too steep, and there was no cell service where he was. He remained beside an air pocket in the crevasse overnight. Meanwhile, when he didn’t check in that evening, his family raised the alarm.

In a recent development, according to a Facebook report by France’s CRS Savoie mountain-rescue unit, they saw the slide path but no immediate sign of Ossatte. The search continued until the middle of the night, when avalanche risk forced the rescuers to suspend their operations.

The following morning, a large contingent of 28 ground rescuers, dogs, three helicopters, and a physician to tend to Ossatte, if they found him alive, converged on the site, according to France 3. They found his gear and dug for five hours until they heard him calling out.

“He was really lucky,” remarked Major Yoann Haberey of the mountain-rescue team. “We knew he was under there. But we didn’t think we’d find him alive.”.

Industry observers note that by the time they extracted him, he had been there almost a day and a half. The hypothermic but lucky survivor was flown to the hospital for treatment and surgery on one of his legs.

  • Industry observers note that the Headwall section of Cerro Torre.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As the title suggests, Behind the Climb brings viewers behind the scenes with Colin Haley and Tyler Karow as they take on the Southeast Ridge of Cerro Torre. Colin Haley has tried the route, which he calls a modern classic, three times already without success. He hopes that by teaming up with Tyler Karow, the fourth time will be the charm.

As the short film opens, Haley introduces us to the route in voiceover, while on-screen, he and Karow make the approach, crossing ice fields and fording streams. The route is divided into three main sections: the Haston Crack, Ice Towers, and Headwall. Haley was turned back twice by bad weather on the Ice Towers; neither of them has finished the Headwall.

Industry observers note that the Headwall section of Cerro Torre. Photo: Screenshot.

Industry observers note that hoping to catch the Ice Towers still frozen and the Headwall still warmed by the sun, they wake up so early that the sun hasn’t actually finished setting yet. At that point, it seems more accurate to say that they took an evening nap and then climbed through the night.

According to recent reports, interspersed with clips of climbing, Haley and Karow review the footage, sharing the little logistical details and impressions of the climb. The Ice Towers, which Karow recalls attempting many years ago, have changed since he last encountered them. Once, as the name implies, thick with ice, much of it has now melted. “In another ten years,” Karow predicts, they will “look drastically different.”.

Industry observers note that ice or no, they complete the second section. This time, the weather cooperates. Haley takes over for the final section, the dastardly Headwall which has repeatedly eluded him. The climbing itself is going well, but melting snow above is making the rock run with water. This, he admits, is a significant disadvantage to their carefully timed initiative.

Despite the wet holds, Haley makes good progress. With only a few pitches to go, the self-described pessimist Haley admits that he finally thinks they’ll make it to the top. When he does finally reach the summit, grinning widely at the camera, voiceover reveals he has already started worrying about the descent.

Keeping with the promise to go behind the scenes, the video doesn’t stop at the summit, where they stand victoriously and admire the views. We follow the pair as they rappel down.

At the bottom, when asked how they feel about the adventure, both men reply simply that their hands hurt. Not all of us can be poets.

#68050. Jetboil TrailCook 2.0L Stove Review: The Ultimate Stove for Group Backpacking Trips

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2402 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Jetboil TrailCook 2.0L Stove Review: The Ultimate Stove for Group Backpacking Trips

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2402 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Over the years, my backcountry cook setup has run the gamut from no-cook options to cooking for 12+ people on multiday treks across the Sierra Nevada or Grand Canyon.
  • In a recent development, on solo thru-hikes like the Pacific Crest Trail and Colorado Trail, I have historically used my trusted BRS stove to get the job done.
  • In a recent development, cooking as a guide involves much more than boiling a pot of water to rehydrate a meal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Over the years, my backcountry cook setup has run the gamut from no-cook options to cooking for 12+ people on multiday treks across the Sierra Nevada or Grand Canyon.

In a recent development, on solo thru-hikes like the Pacific Crest Trail and Colorado Trail, I have historically used my trusted BRS stove to get the job done. And by job I usually just mean boiling water or, if I’m lucky during resupply, “cooking” tortellini. However, now as a backcountry guide I find myself cooking for other people much more often than just myself.

In a recent development, cooking as a guide involves much more than boiling a pot of water to rehydrate a meal. Instead of ramen or Knorr sides, we are cooking things like egg sandwiches for breakfast, quesadillas with cilantro salsa for lunch, and backcountry fried teriyaki tofu with mixed veggies for dinner. So with all due respect to my original system, the BRS is not going to cut it out there when I’m trying to fry eggs or crisp up the edges of tofu.

These meals might sound elaborate, but they’re quite simple in the backcountry as long as you have the proper tools: I tested the Jetboil TrailCook 2.0L stove system this summer to see if it could get the job done.

According to recent reports, jetboil has really outdone itself with this one. Highlights include a do-it-all pot that’s large enough to feed the whole group, light enough to carry on the trail, and built with much of the same technology Jetboil users already know and love, plus key improvements over past models.

Straining boiling water into a larger pot while cooking for a large group on the Lost Coast Trail. The TrailCook 2.0L would soon after be used to soft boil some eggs.

MSRP: $199 Weight: 1 lb 6.24 oz or 630 g Dimensions: 17.3 cm x 14.5 cm Boil time:130 sec/0.5 liter water Capacity: 2 liters.

Sources indicate that while I think the Trailcook is one of the best all-in-one cook systems available on the market today, there is a specific use case for this setup. This system is overkill for a solo thru-hiker, but it really shines when you are cooking for more than two people on a backcountry outing. If your idea of camp cooking goes beyond boiling water and into preparing actual meals for you and your friends in the woods, the TrailCook 2.0L is definitely worth a look.

Industry observers note that I took the TrailCook 2.0L system out on several outings during my initial testing period, putting it to work in a variety of group settings. It fed me and my coworkers during a three-day training trip on the Tahoe Rim Trail, helped cook for 18 students over six days in the Gila Wilderness, and performed beautifully while preparing meals for 11 women on the Lost Coast Trail.

It has been revealed that across each of these trips, the TrailCook 2.0L consistently felt like it was the right tool for the job. It never felt bulky or difficult to pack, yet it always had enough capacity to handle the demands of group cooking. What started as a product to test has swiftly become an integral part of my kitchen setup on group trips, and I plan to continue taking it into the backcountry long after this review is published.

Boiling water rapidly while students participate in a field lesson before dinner.

FluxRing: This heat-transfer technology is one reason Jetboil stoves are among the best at heating rapidly and efficiently.

Handling tabs and strainer: These user-friendly features let you drain the pot without burning your fingers on the hot lid. Hole for more exact pours on one side of the lid and strainer lines on the other.

Handling tabs and lid-lifter protected from heat.

Sources indicate that integrated 6,000 BTU/hr Burner: Powerful and effective. Just 130 seconds to boil half a liter of water.

Folding lockout silicone handles: Super handy for when the pot is full of heavy water or food. There is nothing worse than having to guess if your pot handle is going to hold.

It has been revealed that easy-ignite: The Trailcook lights just like a gas stove at home. The igniter felt intuitive and worked every time I used it. Keeping my fingers crossed it continues to do so.

Igniter with precision heat control features.

In a recent development, precision heat control: This was a great feature for simmering or otherwise controlling the stove’s heat level! I haven’t seen this in the previous Jetboil versions I have owned, and I definitely suggest choosing a model with this feature included.

Compatible with accessories: While I didn’t test the stove with any accessories, the Summit Skillet will also fit with this system, as will the 1.5L cookpot, giving you multiple cooking surface options.

Recent findings suggest that all-in-one packing: It’s so notable to have gear that fits well into your pack. Despite this stove system’s large capacity, it’s so compact and easy to fit neatly into a backpack. The burner goes into a small bag, which can fit inside the pot along with a small (4 oz) fuel canister. The lid can then be put on and the handles folded to keep everything neatly packed together.

Stove with igniter and fuel all neatly held inside pot with handles keeping everything together. Hand shown for scale.

It has been revealed that 2Lpot: The size of this pot makes it ideal for large-group cooking, such as on my guided backcountry trips. While a second or third pot might be needed depending on group size, this system always boils water the quickest and gets the cooking off to a quick and easy start.

There are a lot of stoves on the market, but what makes a Jetboil a Jetboil is how quickly it can take water from snowmelt to a rolling boil. It has an insanely fast boil time, and that has undoubtedly contributed to Jetboil’s popularity over the years. When you’re cold, hungry, and ready for dinner, those extra few minutes start to matter.

Sources indicate that the TrailCook 2.0L is designed for group cooking, and where it really stands out is in its combination of speed, efficiency, and packability. There are plenty of ways to cook for a group in the backcountry. For years, my setup was an MSR WhisperLite, a fuel bottle, and a large pot. That system works, but it also means carrying multiple pieces of gear, finding room for all of them in your pack, and waiting longer for water to boil.

The TrailCook 2.0L simplifies all of that. Everything nests neatly together, and thanks to Jetboil’s FluxRing technology, it boils water and cooks food much faster and more efficiently than the WhisperLite setups I’ve used in the past. It’s also not limited to just boiling water. The improved heat control makes it much easier to simmer, sauté, and cook actual meals instead of simply rehydrating food.

Industry observers note that soft-boiling eggs for the group. 6-minute boil followed by rapid cold dunk. Enjoy!

Recent findings suggest that what impressed me most was how much cooking capacity Jetboil packed into such a compact system. A two-liter pot capable of feeding a group could easily feel bulky or awkward to carry, but I never felt like the TrailCook took up an unreasonable amount of pack space. On trips where I was cooking for anywhere from a handful of coworkers to nearly twenty students, I was consistently glad to have it along.

And while the TrailCook is certainly designed with the backcountry in mind, I think it deserves some credit for front-country camping too. If you’re cooking for two to four people, it offers a much more compact and portable alternative to hauling around a traditional Coleman stove and camp kitchen setup. You give up some cooking surface area, but you gain a lot in ease of use, packability, and speed.

I love knowing that when I get to camp after a long day of hiking or driving, my cook system is together in one place and takes just seconds to get going when it’s time to start dinner.

There are so many features on the TrailCook 2.0L that I love. Below is my love note to each of them:.

Locking handles: Glorious. They lock out and feel sturdy and secure while cooking, and I never worried about them folding unexpectedly while moving a pot full of food around camp. A real blessing.

Lid: A design I found myself appreciating over and over again. Having both a pour hole and a built-in strainer makes draining pasta, pouring hot water, or straining veggies incredibly easy. It’s one of those simple features that feels like it was added after years of field testing and experience. It just makes sense.

Strainer side of lid, letting the water out while keeping the yum yum in.

According to recent reports, no boil-over: If you’ve ever stood over a stove trying to prevent starchy pasta water from dumping all over your cook setup, you’ll understand why this is such a win. Even when I filled the pot well above the fill line, the contents didn’t bubble out like they did with some older Jetboil models.

Heat pads: The heat pads built into the lid sound minor, but they’re such a quality-of-life improvement. In the past, dumping water out of the lid usually meant grabbing a buff, a shirt sleeve, or whatever happened to be nearby to avoid burning my fingers on the hot metal. With the TrailCook 2.0L, this is a non-issue thanks to the little orange heat pads.

Speed: This thing is FAST. Jetboil has built its reputation on rapid boil times, and the TrailCook 2.0L is no exception. Whether I was melting snow, boiling water for a meal, or trying to get dinner on the table for a large group, I was consistently impressed by how swiftly it got the job done. It worked so well that I could boil multiple pots of water on the Jetboil before the first pot finished boiling on my Whisperlite when I had both stoves going at once.

Capacity: It was large enough to comfortably cook for groups — including one trip where I was feeding 20 people — without ever feeling excessively bulky in my pack. That’s a tough balance to strike, and this system nailed it.

Recent findings suggest that built-in igniter: Backpacking stoves have come with built-in igniters for years, including Jetboils, but they’re often unreliable and break easily. In contrast, this one worked reliably throughout my testing. When everyone is hungry and waiting for dinner, being able to fire up the stove with the turn of a switch is a beautiful thing. Goodbye, “which pocket is my lighter in again?”.

Heating rapidly is what Jetboil does best.

Pot support system: If I had one criticism of the TrailCook 2.0L, it would be the pot support system. I like the concept of the redesigned support arms and appreciate that the pot can be easily lifted on and off the stove. However, Jetboil markets the system as “self-centering,” and that wasn’t my experience.

I often found it surprisingly difficult to tell whether the pot was properly seated on the support arms. The grooves on the bottom of the pot are supposed to align with the arms on the stove, but there isn’t much tactile or visual feedback to let you know when everything is lined up correctly. More than once, I found myself double-checking the alignment before feeling confident enough to start cooking.

That being remarked, once the pot is properly seated, it feels stable and secure. The problem is getting it there. If one of the support arms misses its groove, the pot can sit unevenly, creating the potential for a spill if you’re not paying attention. It’s not a dealbreaker, but it’s one area where I think the user experience could be improved. I would love some external indication that the arms are in the grooves.

Weight: Again, this system shines in a specific use case. For solo hikers, the 2L capacity and 24 oz weight penalty don’t make sense. This isn’t a knock on the stove itself, which is meant for group trips.

The stabilizing arms shown along with bottom pot ring that sits on top.

Is this stove system worth my $199? My simple answer is yes. It has an overwhelming amount of useful, streamlined features and does the job well every single time. If I were in the market for a large-capacity Jetboil system, the TrailCook 2.0L would have my dollar.

In a recent development, overall, the value-to-spend here is wonderful, but whether it’s worth it to you depends a lot on your use case. Do you need a large-capacity Jetboil system? Would the TrailCook 1.2L be enough capacity for your cooking needs? Do you cook for groups in the backcountry or are you a solo thru-hiker? Let these questions help guide your purchasing decision.

Shop the Jetboil Trailcook 2.0L Stove System.
