#68048. Breaking: Kayaking 3,700km Around Britain

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1691 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Kayaking 3,700km Around Britain

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1691 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, dominic Gribbin, 61, is more than five months into his attempt to circumnavigate mainland Great Britain by sea kayak.
  • Gribbin released his expedition from Crinan Harbour in Argyll, Scotland, on June 2.
  • The journey has not gone according to initiative.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, dominic Gribbin, 61, is more than five months into his attempt to circumnavigate mainland Great Britain by sea kayak. But relentless weather delays and mounting costs have made the journey even more challenging than anticipated.

Gribbin released his expedition from Crinan Harbour in Argyll, Scotland, on June 2. Paddling clockwise, he has covered 2,584km. From Crinan, he continued up the west coast of Scotland and around Cape Wrath and Duncansby Head before heading south along the eastern and southern coasts. His latest reported landing point is Cliff End, near Hastings, Sussex.

The journey has not gone according to initiative. Persistent Atlantic weather systems have cost him weeks of paddling time, while the financial demands of keeping the expedition moving have forced him to return to freelance television camerawork so he and his wife, Nicola, can keep it running.

While he paddles, she follows him in their motor home, offering shore support. He now hopes to complete the circle at Crinan in the spring of 2027. ExplorersWeb caught up with him to find out more about the journey. This interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.

How do you approach the daily distances on a journey like this?

Given that circumnavigating the British mainland is at least 3,700km, I have aimed to do at least 40km per day. My longest day so far has been 64km. However, weather, tides and daylight length, particularly in autumn and winter, often curtail one’s best-laid intends. Some days have been necessarily shorter, forcing me to make an earlier-than-envisaged retreat to shore.

Recent findings suggest that but this is very much a journey, not a race, so we will continue into the spring of 2027. It’s an incredible opportunity to explore every nook and cranny of the GB coastline.

How much has the weather affected your progress?

Roughly 85% of delays have been due to poor weather, 5% to Ministry of Defense firing range timetable restrictions, and 10% to the need for very specific tidal windows to navigate particular sections safely and efficiently. I have never had a delay due to fatigue or the need for a break from the sheer physical nature of this endurance challenge. I have used days when I have inevitably been “weathered-off” to recoup my energy reserves.

For most of the trip, it has been extremely rare to have more than four days of consistently good paddling weather. Setting off from Crinan on June 2 meant we did not enjoy the heat wave experienced in southern Britain. Instead, we lost at least six weeks to poor weather. Constant Atlantic westerly and northwesterly fronts brought wind, rain, and high seas that seemed to permanently batter northwest and northern Scotland throughout June, July, and even into early August. It was one of the great untalked-about weather phenomena of summer 2026. It wasn’t all heat waves…at least not in Scotland!

Are you camping or sleeping in the motorhome?

Northwest Scotland and its wild, deeply indented coastline often made road access to the sea impossible. Early on, we accepted that there would be long stretches when Nicola would not see me for over 24 hours. She was often doing double the mileage I was doing and negotiating some very hairy driving conditions on roads way off the beaten track. That resulted in many planned and unplanned wild camps along the coast.

By the time we reached the north coast of Scotland, road access had improved dramatically, and Nicola and I were generally able to coordinate to meet at the end of each day. This has proved an invaluable motivator, especially when the going gets tough. Our little motorhome has been a blessed retreat each night since then: a warm, reassuring space to relax, gather one’s thoughts, and plan ahead.

Industry observers note that the route so far. The blue line indicates the paddling route, the red line shows the route taken by the support vehicle. Image: Dominic Gribbin.

What kayak are you paddling, and how much equipment do you carry?

I am paddling around Britain in a Rockpool Taran 16 sea kayak. It is a fast, beautifully handmade sea kayak, perfect for putting down the miles and handling heavy seas. The trade-off is stability, but it has a prodigious load capacity in its various watertight bulkheads.

I carry a kayak trolley permanently on the back deck. I have already worn out two and am constantly experimenting with upcoming designs to better negotiate the challenges of gravel and sand beaches. As a minimum, I carry basic wild-camping equipment in case I need to spend an unexpected night ashore.

Food consists of pre-cooked rice bags, canned fish and vegetables, alongside plenty of snacks. I favor savory rather than sweet food. Coffee is my essential luxury, and I normally carry a can or two of beer!

Safety equipment is extensive. I carry a Garmin 86i Marine GPS with InReach satellite tracking, an ICOM marine handheld VHF radio with AIS and GPS, a spare VHF radio, flares and smoke signals, and a McMurdo personal locator beacon. I also carry a fully integrated Garmin Fenix 7 Pro watch, first-aid kit, spare paddles, compass, mobile phone, battery packs, head lamp, repair tape, and a Swiss Army penknife.

Recent findings suggest that the kayak itself weighs 24.9kg, but the overall weight, including my dry suit, buoyancy aid, clothing, and equipment, easily reaches 35kg or more. It is a significant challenge to negotiate all this weight over an often-unfriendly shoreline. However, the kayak benefits from the additional weight when afloat.

What have been the most memorable moments along the way?

In a recent development, we have had numerous encounters with sea otters, hunting pods of bottlenose dolphins, and close-up encounters with bottlenose mothers and calves. There have also been golden eagles and white-tailed sea eagles, the largest raptor in the UK. Some of the most sublime moments have been the inshore sea passages through the sheltered waters of the Inner Hebrides.

Sources indicate that successfully rounding Cape Wrath was a truly intimidating but awe-inspiring milestone. Then there was rounding the infamous Duncansby Head and crossing the Pentland Firth near John O’Groats, finally seeing the compass turn south. The huge breeding seabird colonies off Caithness and much of Scotland’s northeast coast have been incredible. Literally tens of thousands of birds, a deafening cacophony of noise!

Right along the GB coastline, we have also met some of the warmest and most generous people.

Have there been any particularly frightening moments?

In a recent development, the huge seas off Strathy Point, Caithness, are probably the closest call yet. If something had gone wrong there while two kilometers offshore in those seas, I wouldn’t be writing this.

I have experienced plenty of rough and scary seas so far, but that occasion was another order of magnitude. They were enormous seas driven by Arctic swell and spring tides. They were the biggest seas I have ever paddled in. I am not in a rush to return there, despite its beauty.

Industry observers note that you have mentioned that you are now combining freelance work with the expedition. How are you managing the financial and logistical side?

Recent findings suggest that we were able to make this happen because I am self-employed. We bankrolled the expedition using our savings. The motorhome for shore support was the biggest investment. We initially calculated finances based on finishing by mid-autumn, but those weather delays cost us dearly. We ran out of money by mid-September, so I have had to return to my freelance work as a TV cameraman and juggle that with keeping this Edge of Britain expedition going until we are finished.

Recent findings suggest that there is no stopping this winter. Instead, we will take advantage of every weather window.

How did you first get into the sport?

According to recent reports, I began paddling at age 11 when I permanently borrowed a friend’s old kayak and started exploring the ankle-deep waters of the River Ver and River Colne around St. Albans and Park Street, Hertfordshire. At 13, I started British Canoe Union training. This began my lifelong involvement with whitewater paddling on rivers around the world.

In a recent development, back in the 1970s and 1980s, when I began, skills progression was funneled entirely through very actively encouraged participation in canoe slalom. Everybody who learned to paddle at club level was involved in slalom to some degree. I chose men’s C1 (Canadian singles) and competed at a national level, ranking 19th in Great Britain by the age of 18.

Sources indicate that university changed my orientation somewhat, and the allure of traveling to exotic whitewater rivers around the world took over. Expedition whitewater paddling then became my life, and still is, alongside expedition sea kayaking. Combining this with filmmaking ultimately led directly to my career as a television cameraman.

Why did you decide to take on a circumnavigation of Britain?

The decision to attempt to paddle around the GB mainland is the culmination of a life spent kayaking. It is hard not to fall in love with the sheer beauty and allure of the world of the river and coastline, particularly here at home in the UK. This country has what is widely celebrated as some of the best sea kayaking in the world. To dream of exploring the whole GB coastline in as much detail as time and weather allow is, to me, a logical conclusion.

In a recent development, the actual decision came extremely late in the day, namely January 2026. This began a frantic period of organization ahead of our June 2 launch. Admittedly, April would have been better, but prior commitments meant we had to begin in June.

According to recent reports, I chose a clockwise route around Britain, thinking (naively) that the prevailing winds would vaguely be behind us for at least half the journey. I also wanted to tackle the potentially most technically demanding section of the northwest and north coast of Scotland early, in the height of what I envisaged as long summer days. How wrong I was!

  • Last week, high winds forced the Russian team to retreat from their third trip up the West Ridge of Everest.
  • “We are at Lobuche…resting, analyzing the weather forecast.
  • Sources indicate that in a post on social media, member Sergey Kondrashkin recalls the latest trip up.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last week, high winds forced the Russian team to retreat from their third trip up the West Ridge of Everest. Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and leader Andrei Vasiliev were climbing without oxygen, with no one else on the mountain. Winter is quickly approaching, but they have no intention of going home yet.

“We are at Lobuche…resting, analyzing the weather forecast. Still want to try again,” Vasiliev texted to ExplorersWeb over the weekend. The climbers had not intended to reach the summit on that latest attempt up the West Shoulder of Everest via the Lho La Pass. Vasiliev explained that they were not yet acclimatized enough to reach the top without bottled oxygen. They did expect to reach higher than before, but high winds made that impossible.

Sources indicate that in a post on social media, member Sergey Kondrashkin recalls the latest trip up. On November 11, the team set off from their tent at the base of the West Ridge, fixing ropes in bitterly cold temperature. Contrary to forecasts, winds were light. The climbers pitched their tent at 6,500m and still had time to fix some ropes above them.

On the following morning, however, the gusts were too strong. After waiting in vain for the gale to abate, and with a forecast of even stronger winds the following day, Kondrashkin returned to the ridge, trying not to be blown away. He advanced between gusts and retrieved his two ice axes and the rope he had left behind the day before. They would need that gear for the descent.

Once at the bivouac, the climbers retrieved their tent, cached some food and fuel, and downclimbed to their Camp 1 at some 5,600m. It lies on the steep section between the Khumbu Glacier and the Lho La. Here, they pitched their tent again.

On Friday, the Russian team rappelled down to the glacier, on a “relatively safe” line to the right, where an avalanche fell as they descended.

Recent findings suggest that today, the team sits at their lodge in Lobuche and looks intently at weather forecasts. “We have not yet decided when to return to the mountain,” Vasiliev told Explorersweb. “It’s all about the weather, and the forecasts announce high winds on November 20-21.”.

#68044. The Not So Spiritual Camino Variant

📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

The Not So Spiritual Camino Variant

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1125 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today marked Stage 2 of the Variante Espiritual, which we decided to hike in reverse.
  • I woke up early to enjoy the solitude of breakfast on the patio with front-row views of the water.
  • Sources indicate that at 8:00 AM, we stepped out into a cold breeze blowing across the water.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today marked Stage 2 of the Variante Espiritual, which we decided to hike in reverse. After days of walking against the main flow of pilgrims, yesterday was the first time we had the trail mostly to ourselves—aside from the crowds packing onto the upriver boats.

I woke up early to enjoy the solitude of breakfast on the patio with front-row views of the water. Watching the sun light up the morning sky with a plate of boiled quail eggs and a couple of strong cups of espresso was a wonderfully peaceful start. Today was billed as one of the most scenic and spiritual sections of the entire Camino.

Sources indicate that at 8:00 AM, we stepped out into a cold breeze blowing across the water. The sun was just over the horizon, casting warm rays across the long footbridge as we crossed a small inlet bay to hike along the coast.

After walking along the coast for a bit, the trail angled inland. Following a slight climb up to a small church, we made our first wrong turn of the day.

Once we realized we were off the official Camino, we decided to forge our own path using Google Maps rather than backtrack.

The route crossed a high bridge over a busy highway before diving into a peaceful forest. Climbing up, we looked back and were amazed to see how far away the coast already looked. We could see the bay, distant coastal cities, and mountains on the horizon—all after just an hour and a half of walking.

As we exited the trees, we stumbled upon a massive vineyard stretching out across the hills. Unfortunately, the winery wasn’t open for another 20 minutes, so we kept moving. Walking through endless fields of grapes was incredible, and skipping the wine stop turned out to be a blessing given what the trail had in store for us later.

Walking against the grain of the Camino created endless confusion for everyone we passed:.

They became genuinely concerned for us, which we thought was endearing. Every time we ran into a local, we used a mix of butchered Spanish and sign language to explain we were hiking toward Porto. Other times, we just smiled, waved, and kept moving.

We were deep in the countryside, passing beautiful solid-stone homes with immaculate gardens and tiny backyard vineyards.

By mid-morning, we had already knocked out 9 miles in under three hours.

We spotted the only café we’d seen all morning, grabbed a coffee and black tea, and relaxed on the porch overlooking the river. With such a fast pace early on, we assumed the rest of the day would be a breeze. We were very wrong.

Industry observers note that the path ran right alongside the river for the next mile. The water was teeming with huge, two-foot-long fish—an invasive species, I assumed, since the river was practically overflowing with them. As the shade disappeared, the heat began to rise rapidly.

At the junction of two busy multilane highways, we tried crossing via an elevated pedestrian bridge. As we climbed, thick briers started crowding the walkway—a red flag I should have noticed sooner. Reaching the other side, I realized we were totally off-track. We backtracked over the highway and ended up at a massive roundabout packed with nonstop traffic. Fortunately, we spotted a pedestrian tunnel to get us safely across.

On the other side of the highway, we stopped at a small roadside restaurant. This was a crucial stop: there were no grocery stores, cafés, or towns along our next stretch of the route.

We ordered the local Pilgrim’s Menu:.

Before leaving, I refilled our water bottles from the bathroom sink, knowing we were heading into a dry, rural stretch.

The next 5.5 km section was advertised as a tranquil forest trail running along a bubbling river with numerous waterfalls, climbing gently up to the Mosteiro de Santa María da Armenteira.

It has been revealed that since we couldn’t get a room at the monastery, our strategy was to split off the Camino early and head to our accommodation in the tiny village of Silva. Armed with Google Maps, I figured it would be an easy shortcut.

Hot, tired, and out of water, we took a brief breather in a shaded cove when a cool breeze finally offered a moment of relief.

After climbing along the creek for 5 km, we left the Camino to forge our own path to Silva.

What started as a narrow, paved road quickly turned into a steep, unpaved logging trail climbing straight up through the forest. On Google Maps, it looked like a legitimate road; in reality, it was an overgrown, barely used dirt track.

I started to question: were we climbing all this way just to hit a dead end and be forced to hike all the way back down?

According to recent reports, knockerz was melting, I was completely exhausted, and we were both soaked in sweat and desperately thirsty. I hit that dazed, survival-mode state where you just keep putting one foot in front of the other, hoping the hill ends soon.

Industry observers note that we kept pushing up the incline until, suddenly, the dirt track broke through the trees and met a paved road leading right to our door. Google Maps had come through.

Our lodging was a small, unmanned albergue with eight rooms and a shared kitchen.

Upon arrival our first stop was to hydrate. We went straight into the shared kitchen and drank glass after glass of cold water.

Next stop was to shower. We each took showers with our clothes on to rinse the caked-on sweat and dirt off both our bodies and gear at the same time.

Laying in the bed we were glad this day was done.

According to recent reports, after decades of no backpacking an abrupt life incident forced me back into the woods for some shinrin-yoku where I ran into a NOBO tramily at Shuckstack Fire Tower. That started an idea of a longer term forest bath on the AT. What a long strange trip its been. Any financial donations I get will be used to send out love to other thru hikers a trail magic.

Officials Blame Climate Change for Glacier Collapse That Killed 17

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (340 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Russian authorities are now attributing the September 6 disaster on 5,047m Mount Mizhirgi in the northern Caucasus to climate-related destabilization of a hanging glacier.
  • Recent findings suggest that A half-million cubic meter avalanche struck a military group undergoing mountain training, killing 17 and injuring 10.
  • Industry observers note that the impact generated a powerful blast of displaced air that reportedly threw some victims 200m to 300m down the slope before burying them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Russian authorities are now attributing the September 6 disaster on 5,047m Mount Mizhirgi in the northern Caucasus to climate-related destabilization of a hanging glacier.

Recent findings suggest that A half-million cubic meter avalanche struck a military group undergoing mountain training, killing 17 and injuring 10. Another 10 were unharmed and made it down the mountain on their own.

Industry observers note that the impact generated a powerful blast of displaced air that reportedly threw some victims 200m to 300m down the slope before burying them. As we reported at the time, helicopter pilot Alexander Davydov caught the avalanche on video.

According to recent reports, eldar Khashkhozhev of the Russian Ministry of Emergency Situations explained that warmer temperatures melted the protective blanket of snow, exposing parts of the glacier. This weakened the ice support that had glued enormous masses of snow and ice in place for decades.

A helicopter inspection of the region’s snow conditions the month before found no cause for concern, and some officials insist the catastrophe was unpredictable. However, climber Dmitry Polyakov, who was in the region at the time, disputed the idea that the glacier posed no danger. He said climbers had long recognized its instability and generally avoided approaching it in large groups.

The Mizhirgi Glacier against Mizhirgi East and West peaks, site of September’s catastrophic glacial collapse. Photo: Shutterstock.

The key points of Khashkhozhev’s explanation were:.

Rising temperatures have raised the altitude of permanent snow cover.

Previously protected sections of the glacier became exposed, weakening the supporting ice beneath the hanging masses.

Eventually, gravity overcame that support and triggered a collapse that struck the training group.

This was the largest climbing disaster in the country since 2002, when another glacier collapse in North Ossetia, located between the Black and Caspian Seas, killed 125 people, including local residents.

With major landslides in summer and the possibility of glacial collapse at other times of the year throughout the world, mountaineers will have to adjust their behavior, as previously safe areas become potentially deadly.
